The DGV manual of procedures is under review and new training will be provided shortly to all staff responsible for the supervision of the rendering plants. _______________________ 14

To implement the plan for the eradication of sheep and goat brucellosis as agreed with the Commission services ­ in particular to discontinue re-vaccination of adult animals and to implement the serological testing of vaccinated adult animals in Trás-os-Montes.

audits.title: Illegal Imports of products of animal origin and live animals

recommendations.text: Background Customs are responsible for personal baggage checks of travellers in all points of entry. They check all points of entry including daily checks in the existing post centre and the express mail centre in the airport. ¾ No specific training was provided in the field of veterinary checks and checks for illegal imports of veterinary consignments.

Information to passengers/travellers ¾ The posters displayed in the BIP-airport visited contain all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. However, no such information was displayed in the ports and there was no detailed knowledge for the other airports. ¾ Different leaflets prepared by customs or by DGV were available at the BIP- airport visited; however, they do not contain all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. ¾ No further initiatives were taken in order to increase public awareness as no information reflecting the provisions of the above Regulation is distributed to the passengers in aircrafts or ships. There was no responsibility defined to ensure that airline operators or shipping lines inform their passengers accordingly; it was not clarified, if e.g. in-flight-announcements are made. 5.2.2.3.Organisation of controls/sanctions ¾ Customs are permanently present in every point of entry from third countries either BIP or non-BIP. Customs stated that in case of the airports all arriving flights from third countries in all points of entry are checked by customs and international flights from other EU airports are checked in the same way as the passengers come through the same channel. ¾ In this framework no priority is given to veterinary products as these are included in the general illegal imports checks. Customs stated that checks are carried out for all illegal imports on a risk based approach. The criteria for risk analyses varied between flights from different countries and each point of entry has its own criteria. ¾ There are no records for cases of consignments seized as they were not abandoned by passengers in the whole country. The same applies for CITES- consignments for which the CCA did not have an overview for the seized consignments of live animals and products of animal origin. ¾ Passengers are not liable for the cost of destruction of seized consignments nor for any penalties laid down in Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, if the 4 illegal consignments are abandoned or seized after being discovered by customs. Customs believes that seizure of the relevant consignments is adequate sanction and they do not consider that the attempt for illegal import is smuggling. ¾ There was no list of points of entry from third countries and CCA stated that there are no non-BIP-airport-entry-points for passengers with baggage arriving directly from third countries or from third countries through other EU airports (interline). At a BIP-airport-entry-point (Lisboa airport) customs use scanning equipment to check selected baggage. Sniffer dogs are not employed to check specifically for products of animal origin. ¾ Regarding veterinary products flights from South American countries and Africa have the highest priority. ¾ As part of their integrated controls customs checks physically about 20 % of luggage from all flights from third countries. As customs are not allowed to open the luggage, they have to hold it back and open it in the presence of the owner. In case of reinforced control for a high risk origin customs increase the percentage to e.g. 70 % for flights from Guinea-Bissau. In approximately 50 % of cases of physical checks customs find prohibited goods; however, the percentage of products of animal origin and live animals among these 50 % could not be clarified as requested. ¾ There are two scanners but the amount of the luggage scanned could not be clarified as requested. They are used mainly to scan the transit luggage and to scan luggage at the green channel of the airport. ¾ Customs stated that interline luggage of passengers from third countries with stopover in other EU airports is checked at the destination airport in Portugal, whereas the hand baggage is checked on the first airport of the EU. The interline luggage is scanned in Lisboa airport, mainly for security reasons. No lists of the arriving passengers are received and the physical luggage check is based on random selection at the green channel from the colour-coded tags of the luggage. ¾ According to customs seizures are also a criteria for their risk analysis and a report of all seizures was present in Lisboa airport. However, no overview of the seized consignments of products of animal origin and live animals for 2003 was available. ¾ There was an overview of seizures of CITES consignments of live animals, provided from the responsible "Ministéro do Ambiente e Ordenamento do Território" for 2003 and 26 vultures, which were sent for quarantine to France, 2 apes, which were sent to zoos but it could not be clarified by CCA, if these were approved under Council Directive 92/65/EEC(i) and 22 birds. ¾ The seized consignments were collected in two secured waste bins under customs control; however, although it was stated in the opening meeting, that there were amnesty bins for passengers voluntarily abandoning products of animal origin, these were not in place, as the airport authorities removed them due to security reasons. Customs stated that passengers have the possibility to hand over relevant products to customs, which never happened. ¾ Seized consignments are incinerated; however, customs could not provide confirmation for the adequate disposal of the seized consignments. CAs did not 5 clarify if the incinerator used for the destruction of the consignments is approved in accordance to Art. 12 of Council Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002(j). At a BIP-port-entry-point (Lisboa port) customs use scanning equipment to check luggage. There are no sniffer dogs trained for products of animal origin. ¾ Customs stated that 100 % of the luggage of cruise ship passengers leaving the ship is scanned and opened. Up to now, no products of animal origin for human consumption were found. In 2004 one consignment with ivory was detected. ¾ No details were provided about the checks carried out in other port-entry- points, which could have possible traffic with passengers from third countries. There was no passenger traffic at the non-BIP-port-entry-point visited. 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight ¾ The selection of the consignments subject to veterinary checks is not completely reliable and consignments may escape veterinary checks as relevant customs databases are not linked completely with the requirements for veterinary checks, in particular for consignments under customs transit procedure. ¾ At the BIP-airport-entry point almost 100 % of consignments are customs released for importation and a 100 % documentary check is carried out. Based on a risk analysis (origin of goods, importer, declarant, itinerary, product, customs destination) a 10 ­ 12 % physical check is carried out by opening these consignments; no scanners are used. No information was available how often veterinary goods were detected but not declared as such. ¾ At the non-BIP-port-entry point: around 10 % of the consignments are customs released for importation and 90 % are under customs transit procedure. After the customs procedure is opened, 100 % of the consignments for importation are subjected to a documentary check. 30 ­ 40 % of the consignments released for importation are subjected to physical checks. These are chosen on the basis of the product and the origin. 5 % of the consignments under customs transit procedure are physically checked. Since 31.05.2004 no non-declared container with products of animal origin has been found. ¾ At the BIP-port-entry point: around 90 % of the consignments are customs released for importation and 10 % are under customs transit procedure, mainly to Spain. After the customs procedure is opened, 100 % of the consignments for importation are subjected to documentary checks. Physical checks are based on risk analysis taking into consideration the importer, type of goods and their origin, history and flow of traffic. Drugs are considered to be the main risk and South American countries are checked with highest priority. The percentages for checks on transit consignments could not be provided. In October 2004 around 29 % of the imported consignments were physically checked. ¾ There are between 14.000 ­ 15.000 import declarations/year and 87 consignments (around 0,6 %)were found in 2004 which did not match the description of the goods; however, no products of animal origin were involved. ¾ There are presently no scanners for containers in place, but it is planned to buy two in 2005 which will be placed in the two major ports in Portugal. Other general findings were the following: ¾ There were no details of checks and seized consignments found inland by customs or the DGFCQA for 2003 for freight consignments. 6 ¾ Customs stated that in customs warehouses no consignments of animal origin were found in 2004 which were not declared as such. No results are received of the checks carried out by the "Anti Fraud Department". ¾ In cases, when consignments are sent to a customs warehouse in Portugal in the same customs district, customs at the port keep the original CVED and it does not follow the consignment to the first place of destination as foreseen in Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004(k). 5.2.4. Import of post consignments Customs are permanently present in the post office in Lisboa which is one point of entry for mail, packages or parcels; there are other points of entry in the Autonomous Regions. Live animals cannot to be sent by post under the "Postal Convention" but for products of animal origin basically nothing is prohibited. ¾ No positive list was present and the involved parties in the post office were not aware of prohibitions for products of animal origin(4). ¾ Consignments send by TNT or DHL arrive with airway bills and they are checked by customs in the express mail centre in the airport(5). ¾ The main criteria to check express mail, packages or parcels is the value and consignments below 22 Euro are generally not opened as they are not taxed. Approximately 15 % of the urgent mail and 10 ­ 15 % of parcels are taxed. The selection for post consignments to be physically checked is based on its content, origin, destination and experience of the staff carrying out the risk assessment. ¾ Until 11.09.2004 a scanner had been available. There are no sniffer dogs, which would be considered to be useful for the detection of tinned and canned consignments. ¾ The CA for products of animal origin was not clearly defined and the mission team was told, in case of problems concerning food, the DGFCQA, concerning eggs and CITES, the DGV and concerning hunting trophies, the authority responsible for CITES would be contacted. ¾ For the consignments with products of animal origin with a weight of less then 4 kg a stamp of the DGFCQA on the customs document and for consignments above 4 kg the authorisation from DGFCQA is required. As there were no third country lists present and as DGFCQA did not provide further information on these checks, it is not clear if the system complies with the provisions laid down in Art. 16 (1b) of Directive 97/78/EC. ¾ There was no clear overview of the number of consignments of products of animal origin received by post as no records are kept from the outcome of the physical checks. Different information from different persons involved in the control process were received and it varied from 3 - 4 consignments per year to 1 consignment per week. (4) In their comments to the draft report DGAIEC stated, that the sorting office in Lisboa is equipped with computers linked to the general network of the "Ministry of Finances" and thus have access to the internet and paper versions of the Working Tariff, including any updates. (5) In their comments to the draft report DGAIEC stated, that for express mail, physical checks cover the entire consignment, with the exclusion of those containing only documents. 7 6. ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7374/2004 In response to the findings in the draft report, DGAIEC indicated the following: Legislative and administrative measures under point 5.1.2: This has already been addressed, since the list of customs warehouses authorised to receive products of animal origin and the organisational structure of DGAIEC was then sent by fax to DGV, for forwarding to the appropriate Commission department. Co-operation between different authorities under point 5.1.3: The comments made concerning report DG (SANCO) 7046/2004, in point 5.1.5 paragraphs 1 and 4, apply to the issues raised here. Concerning the existence of possible agreements, DGAIEC intends to conclude formal cooperation agreements with DGV. Import and transit of freight under point 5.2.3: Goods placed under the customs warehousing procedure remain subject to controls by the competent customs and veterinary authorities and DGAIEC will take steps to streamline this operation and will work with the veterinary authorities on a more effective method for controls. Import of post consignments under point 5.1.2: If products of animal origin (e.g. dried fish) are sent, they will always be inspected by the competent authority, i.e. the BIP at Lisbon airport.

audits.title: Animal Welfare on farms and during sea transport

recommendations.text: Amend legislation so that a. The minimum standards apply to all pigs confined for rearing and fattening as laid down in Article 1 of Directive 91/630/EEC. b. Article 1, 2(a) Annex, Chapter I, Section I of the Decree 135/2003 concerning the unobstructed floor area is applicable to holdings as laid down in Article 3, 1(a) of 91/630/EC.
To ensure that appropriate training courses are available to pig farmers as required by Article 5a of Directive 61/630/EEC.

To take measures to improve enforcement actions when deficiencies are detected. In particular, punitive measures need to be taken in a timely manner where inappropriate systems have been installed after the deadline of 1.1.2003 (Directive 99/74/EC, Chapter II Article 5, 2 and Article 3 of Directive 61/630/EEC) and where recurring problems such as overstocking are detected (Directive 99/74/EC, Chapter II, Art. 5, 1).
Take measures, such as implementing the previous commitment to carry out quality control of inspectors, so that all aspects of EU legislation are adequately inspected.

Regarding checks of pig holdings, take measures: a. So that holdings built or rebuilt after 1.1.2003 meet EU requirements, in particular Article 3 (1b), (2), (4) and (5) of Directive 91/630/EEC. b. So that, as previously recommended in report 1022/1999, requirements applicable to tail-docking and environmental enrichment are addressed (Directive 91/630/EEC, Annex, Chapter I, 4 and 8). c. So that sick or injured pigs are dealt with appropriately (Chapter II, D of Directive 91/630 and point 4 of the Annex of Directive 98/58/EC).

Regarding checks of holdings with laying hens, take measures: a. So that the appropriate space requirements are applied (Directive 99/74/EC, Chapter II, Art. 5, 1) and inappropriate checklists are taken out of use. b. So that obstacles in the cages are taken into account when measuring cage height (Directive 99/74/EC, Chapter II, Art. 5, 4) c. To prevent forced moulting which does not meet the requirements of Article 3 of Council Directive 99/74/EC and points 11, 14, 15 and 16 of the Annex of Council Directive 98/58/EC, and where such practices are found to be unsatisfactory, to apply appropriate punitive measures. 10

Regarding transport of animals by sea, and as previously recommended in reports 3311/2001 and 9039/2003, take steps to ensure: a. That there is adequate protection against weather and sea (point 18 Chapter I.D of the Annex of Council Directive 91/628/EEC); b. That an instrument for emergency slaughter is available on board (point 23 Chapter I.D of the Annex of Council Directive 91/628/EEC). ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)7544/2005 In their comments on a draft version of this report, the CCA provided the following initial reaction to the recommendations. In relation to 1b, a proposal to amend legislation will be submitted for Government assessment and approval and it is estimated that this should be published before the end of the year. In the meantime, the necessary corrections will be distributed through associations in the sector and the Regional Directorates a 5 (a) also considered in this context. In relation to 2, a request has been made to the certification body of the Ministry of Agriculture to define, in collaboration with the CCA, the structure, content and number of hours for these courses. In the meantime, we will continue to encourage the various bodies, particularly production associations, to organise training courses. In relation to 3, this was already discussed in a meeting of the CPSIPA and the CCA and the methodology agreed and measures in this area will be stepped up. In relation to 4, theoretical and practical training for inspectors and work to standardise criteria and procedures work will continue subject to the availability of human and material resources. In relation to 5b, an information leaflet will be produced and furthermore, before the end of this year it is planned to publish a handbook of best practice for pig farmers in which these issues will be addressed in more detail. In relation to 6a, once the computer application is operational, checks will no longer be made with reference to 450cm2/bird/cage. In relation to 6c, methods which respect the provisions of Directive 98/58/EC will be encouraged. In relation to 7a, all the relevant companies and authorities have been informed about this matter. Although ships masters have reported needing to stow containers, under certain circumstances, so that the stability of the vessel is not compromised, official veterinarians have also been instructed to prevent this type of stowage and initiate infringement proceedings as appropriate. In relation to 7b, all ships are now equipped with a captive bolt gun. 11
Should ensure the allocation of further human and financial recourses to enable full implementation of EU legislation within the scope of the mission.

Should ensure that inspections and other control measures including sample checks and testing (qualitative and quantitative), as appropriate, are carried out to ensure compliance with Regulation (EC) No. 1830/2003 as stipulated by Article 9.
Should consider defining clearly the responsibilities of regional CAs for control activities for the implementation of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003.
Should take account of Commissio 2004/787/EC for sampling food and feed for GMO analysis.

Should ensure that quantitative analysis is carried out by the CA in the cases of positive findings of GMO analyses to allow an assessment as to whether the thresholds defined in Article 24 and 47 of Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003 have been exceeded.

Should ensure that official GMO analysis is performed by laboratories complying with the general criteria of ISO 17025 as required by Article 3(1) of Council Directive 93/99/EC. 21 An action plan in response to these recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within two months of the dispatch of the final report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address these recommendations. 10. ADDENDUM In their response to the draft report the Portuguese authorities provided corrections and clarifications. In their response to the recommendations they indicated that additional resources and measures would be considered to strengthen compliance with EU legislation. 22
To ensure that fallen animals are correctly disposed of as required by Art. 5 of the ABP Regulation.

To ensure that adequate arrangements and sufficient infrastructure are in place for the handling of ABP in the retail, milk and food processing sectors and in certain ABP plants, particularly technical, oleochemical, incineration, composting and biogas plants (Art. 3 of the ABP Regulation). With regard to the CA
To ensure effective and efficient coordination between all the CA involved in the ABP chain, as laid down in Art. 4 (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To pursue measures already in place to ensure that all relevant staff are aware of all provisions they have to enforce throughout the ABP chain. With regard to legal provisions

To ensure that legal implementing provisions to guarantee compliance with the requirements of the ABP Regulation enter into force as a matter of urgency. With regard to the approval of ABP plants and other premises

To ensure that ABP plants are approved in a timely fashion once the legal implementing provisions are available, in accordance with the requirements set out in Chapters III and IV of the ABP Regulation.
To ensure validation of processing plants and approval of processing method 7 as set out in Annex V to the ABP Regulation.

To ensure that certain operators are authorised by the CA where required, in accordance with Art. 2 of Regulation (EC) No 92/2005, and Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 79/2005. 13 With regard to official controls
To ensure that all stages of the ABP chain are subject to adequate, effective and coordinated official controls.

To enhance measures already in place to ensure compliance with requirements on identification and commercial documents, as laid down in Annex II to the ABP Regulation. __________________ 14 ADDENDUM RESPONSE OF THE COMPETENT AUTHORITIES TO THE RECOMMENDATIONS Comments from the Portuguese CCA on the draft report were received on 5 July 2006, and it was indicated that the recommendations are being considered and discussed in order to implement actions in response to them. 15

audits.title: Controls on Feed and compliance with requirements for Feed Hygiene

recommendations.text: To urgently designate the CAs responsible for official controls of the feed chain, including for primary producers, in accordance with Art. 4(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 19

audits.title: Import Controls and Border Inspection Posts

recommendations.text: To complete transposition of Directive 97/78/EC, in particular with regard to the clarification of approval procedures for proposed BIPs to ensure that those are implemented in accordance with Art. 6 of Directive 97/78/EC.

To review all instructions and manuals in order to ensure that there is sufficiently clear guidance to allow correct implementation of the supervision of non-EU complying consignments in customs warehouses and ship suppliers, of rejected consignments, of kitchen waste and of personal baggage checks in order to ensure adequate control and verification as required by Art. 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To take measures in order to clarify the responsibilities between different authorities so that overlapping in certain areas is avoided and the EU provisions are correctly applied.

With respect to the application of Artt. 3 of Directive 97/78/EC and Directive 91/496/EEC to review what measures are necessary regarding the CITES list in order to ensure that all CITES-consignments which are subject to veterinary checks are only introduced through entry points with an appropriately approved BIP.

To further develop the system of supervision to include all BIPs, customs warehouses and ship suppliers, also in order to assess adequately how veterinary import procedures are applied in individual BIPs, customs warehouses and ship suppliers and in order to detect and correct any deficiencies noted, in order to achieve compliance with EU requirements laid down in Directives 97/78/EC and 91/496/EEC and implementing Regulations and Decisions.

To increase the number of staff at the BIPs Lisboa and Porto in order to ensure that all necessary checks are adequately carried out and to be in compliance with the third indent of Annex II to Directive 97/78/EC. 18
To ensure that the list of warehouses and ship suppliers is updated in accordance to Artt. 12 (4) and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC and Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

To take measures to ensure the correct application of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 in relation to the identified inconsistencies in particular for the destruction of illegal imports, mass screening and in the provision of information to travellers described in Art.3 of the aforementioned Regulation in all entry points.
To ensure that correct information is entered into TRACES in accordance with Regulations (EC) No 136/2004 and 282/2004 and Decision 2004/292/EC.
Measures should be put in place to ensure that all necessary records are kept and updated documentation is provided at the BIPs as requested in sections 3 and 4 of the Annex of Decision 2001/812/EC.

To ensure that the requirements for collection, transport and records for destruction of kitchen waste from international means of transport are implemented as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002. recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that legislation is in place giving legal power for the CA to enforce FBO sampling in order to fully implement the SNCP in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 646/2007.
The CA should ensure that CA supervision in poultry establishments, in particular follow-up is effective and appropriate to ensure quality and consistency of official control.

The CA should ensure that when samples for official control are taken sampling plan (number of unit comprising the sample) should respect requirements established in Chapter I of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 or other internationally accepted rules or protocols.
The CA should ensure that appropriate measures are taken and adequate follow-up is carried out in slaughterhouses when repeated non-compliances are identified in poultry establishments.

The CA should gather the necessary data in order to be able to evaluate the progress made under the SNCP, and for the SNCP to be reviewed, in line with Article 5.3 (d) of Regulation (EC) No 2160/2003.

recommendations.text: To implement immediately further measures in order to ensure that pre-notification is 2. provided in advance of the arrival of the consignment on EU territory including complete pre-notification for transhipments in accordance to Art 3 of Directive 97/78/EC, Art. 3 of Directive 91/496/EEC, Art. 2 of Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Art. 1 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004. To keep records and documentation for the relevant consignments in ICs. To further develop the system for the reduced frequency of physical checks in order to ensure that the minimum frequencies are followed per type of product and per third country as required in Art. 1 of Decision 94/360/EC. 13. To ensure that effective deterrent measures are applied in order to ensure satisfactory action is taken for the correction of shortcomings. audits.title: Organic production and labelling of organic products

recommendations.text: Ensure that all staff of the competent authorities performing official controls receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently and to carry out official controls in a consistent manner as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Ensure that CBs have the expertise, equipment and infrastructure required to carry out the tasks delegated to them as required by Article 27(5)(b)(i) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and in particular that CBs have access to appropriate laboratories for testing.
Ensure that all retailers selling organic products to the final consumer have submitted their undertaking to the control system as required by Article 28(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Ensure that PPPs are only used in cases of an established threat to a crop and that only PPPs authorised for use in organic production are used in accordance with Article 12(1)(h) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.
Ensure that controls of operators in respect of the obligation established by Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are effective and appropriate as required by Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
Ensure that the measures necessary to comply with Article 23 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are taken into account including appropriate controls of organic products at market level.

Ensure that the control system as set up allows for the traceability of each product at all stages of production, preparation and distribution as required by Article 27(13) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Ensure that exemptions granted under Article 47 point (c) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are in relation to a specific area by individual operators and only after appropriate verification that forage production is lost.

Ensure that the competence to grant exceptions, as referred to in Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, is not delegated to CBs unless this is provided for in the specific conditions as laid down by the Commission in accordance with Article 22(3) of the same Regulation and as required by Article 27(7)(b) of the same Regulation.

Ensure that import authorisations referred to in Article 19 of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 are only granted for products imported from third countries which are not included in the list referred to in Article 33(2) of of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and if the assessment of the evidence provided by the importer shows that the conditions referred to in Article 33(1)(a) and (b) are fulfilled.

Ensure that consignments of organic products imported from TCs are released for free circulation in the Community only if the requirements of Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 are fulfilled and, in particular, after verification of the consignment by the relevant MS's authority and the endorsement of the certificate of inspection in accordance with paragraph 8 and completion of box 18 of the certificate by the first consignee in accordance with paragraph 9 of the same Article.
Ensure that procedures for import controls of organic products are established in accordance with Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004

Ensure that there is efficient and effective co-ordination between CAs in accordance with Articles 4(3) and (5) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular, with regard to the co-ordination and implementation of the import control system for organic products and between IFAP and GPP.
Ensure effective co-ordination between the delegating CA and the CBs in accordance with Article 27(5)(e) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Ensure that information in any cases of irregularity or infringement affecting the organic status of a product shall be immediately communicated between the CBs, control authorities, CAs and MSs concerned and, where appropriate, to the Commission in accordance with Article 30(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Ensure that where an irregularity is found in regard to compliance with the requirements as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, the CBs shall ensure that no reference to the organic production method is made in the labelling and advertising of the entire lot or production run affected by this irregularity in accordance with Article 30 of the same Regulation.
Ensure that the conditions of Article 27(5) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 are satisfied before control tasks are delegated to a CB.

Ensure that CAs delegating control tasks to CBs shall organise audits or inspections of CBs as necessary and that if, as a result of an audit or an inspection, it appears that such bodies are failing to properly carry out tasks delegated to them, the delegating CA shall withdraw this delegation without delay if the CB fails to take appropriate and timely remedial action as required by Article 27(8) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.
Ensure that the effectiveness of the CBs' controls are regularly verified in accordance with Article 27(9)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

citations.text: In the area of Trás-os-Montes, on a significant number of positive holdings where vaccination coverage was investigated, animals have not been vaccinated as required by Point 4.4.7 of the BMEP.

Movement restrictions are largely applied according to Point 4.4.9 of the BMEP. However, full control and enforcement of movement restrictions of animals from BMNF herds to common pastures is not implemented in areas where 90% of holdings are dependent on common pastures on a daily basis.

The low vaccination coverage on positive holdings in the area of Trás-os-Montes, compromise the overall effectiveness of vaccination in this area. As a consequence the disease frequently occurs in non-immunised animals.

Lack of reliable information on all locations where animals are kept on a permanent or temporary basis prevents full traceability of animals, as well as enforcement and verification of movement restrictions. As not all common pastures are registered, the enforcement of movement restrictions and verification of their effectiveness cannot be fully ensured. Although tracing of movements of animals to common pastures is part of an epidemiological investigation, this information is of limited value because not all new brucellosis outbreaks have been investigated. Failure to fully inforce the movement 14 restrictions and traceability favours the spread and persistence of infections in areas with high disease prevalence, where common pastures have a high impact on disease spread.

There is a lack of procedures to verify on-the-spot implementation of certain control and eradication measures (for example sampling, vaccination, cleaning and disinfection) in order to evaluate their quality, completeness and effectiveness as well as to ensure corrective actions when needed. Thus, the CA cannot demonstrate that activities and measures are implemented as described in the approved programme contrary to the requirement in Article 15.1(a) of Commission Implementing Decision 2013/722/EU.

The CCA has established information systems that support continuous monitoring and evaluation of implementation of the BMEP measures. Desk-top evaluations allow to monitor the indicators of the progress of implementation of the programme (such as number of animals sampled, tested, vaccinated, observation of deadlines). The absence of checks on-the-spot, to evaluate implementation of measures carried out by OPPs (such as sampling and vaccination) as well as lack of verification of implementation of measures such as movement restrictions and cleaning and disinfection on infected holding, preclude the CCA from evaluating the quality, completeness and effectiveness of the specific BMEP measures. This could jeopardise the financial contribution by the Union as the CA might have difficulties demonstrating that activities and measures are implemented as described in the approved programme.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of transporters of ABP/DP check compliance with relevant EU requirements, as set down in Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: Transporters of ABP/DP are inspected annually in order to authorise the containers or trailers used to carry such products, in accordance with national requirements (see finding 8). However, these controls do not include checks on relevant EU requirements including traceability and documentation systems (see finding 23). This is not in line with Article 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

At the transporter of ABP/DP visited, the audit team confirmed that the main focus of the annual official controls is the authorisation of containers and trailers used to carry such products, in accordance with the national rules (see findings 8 and 13) and in practice, no checks are carried out to verify that the relevant EU requirements are fulfilled as required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and Article 32 of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The audit team confirmed that the operator had maintained a comprehensive documentation and traceability system which satisfied the requirements of Article 22 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 and also recorded the sequence of different loads carried. However, the unauthorised use of an ABP tank to transport a food product had been overlooked by the competent authorities.

The checks carried out by the competent authorities to confirm the arrival and dispatch of consignments of ABP/DP in Portugal, combined with the attention paid to traceability and documentation requirements during official controls of most operators in the ABP/DP chain, provides adequate assurances that ABP/DP is used or disposed of in accordance with EU requirements. However, the lack of checks on these and other relevant issues carried out during controls of transporters of ABP/DP undermines the ability of the competent authorities to ensure that the EU requirements are fulfilled throughout the distribution chain. 6

responses.response: The national control plan of ABP establishments, plants and 5 of operators is undergoing adaptation in order to include transporters of ABP/DP, as required by Article 45 of Regulation (EC) n.º 1069/2009. citations.text: In 2015, all male animals were systematically excluded from bTB testing for the purpose of maintenance of OTF herd status in some parts of the country (e.g. where the prevalence of bTB is between 0.2% and 1%). This was not in compliance with the requirements of points 3 and 4.4.2 of the 2015 bTB Programme nor with Annex A(I)(2)(c) to Directive 64/432/EEC. For the purpose of maintenance of OTF herd status, the 2015 national operational instructions on bTB testing requested, for these areas, to test only female animals older than 6 weeks.

The 2016 bTB Programme modified this point. It requires testing of males not intended for fattening and females older than 6 weeks (for the maintenance of OTF herd status in areas where herd prevalence is between 0.2% and 1%). This measure is not fully in line with the requirements of Annex A(I)(2)(c) to Directive 64/432/EEC. For these areas, the 2016 operational instructions on bTB testing instruct that males for breeding older than 6 weeks should also be tested. In one region visited, the OPP coordinating veterinarian stated that only male animals that will, according to the keeper, be kept for breeding will be subject to bTB testing.

Exclusion of male animals from testing in some areas on mainland Portugal may have compromised the maintenance of the OTF herds in these areas in 2015. Also, exclusion of 25% of herds on the mainland from field testing, decreases the ability of the system to detect and eliminate the infected animals as early as possible. As a consequence, the time window for the infection to find another susceptible animal is prolonged as well as the time to finally eliminate the infection. This to some extent explains the continuous persistence of Mycobacterium infection in some areas. This approach decreases the confidence in the true level of bTB infection in cattle population on mainland Portugal and most likely increases the overall long term cost of the eradication efforts. Although animals from fattening herds are subject to slaughterhouse surveillance, due to its limitations, a high number of infected animals may not be detected at the slaughterhouse4.

citations.text: During its visits in public and private green sites where Citrus plants are grown as ornamentals and in Citrus fruit orchards located within or outside the demarcated areas in the North and Central regions the audit team noted that: 13 Larger scale commercial citrus fruit producers and producers of Citrus propagating material routinely implement crop protection schemes for other non-regulated pests of Citrus like citrus leaf miners, scales and aphids. Depending on the degree of aphid infestation, they apply two to four treatments per year. In general, the applications of insecticides by producers of citrus propagating material are far more intensive; The implementation of control measures against T. erytreae, which include insecticide applications, severe pruning on young shoots and destruction of plant debris, is compulsory for Citrus trees and other host plants grown within the infested zone of the demarcated area. DRAPN stated that after the detection of the pest in the Porto metropolitan area, it was not possible to carry out any systematic monitoring of ca. 35,000 private properties such as backyard gardens, where owners are often absent; In one case examined in detail, Citrus trees grown as ornamentals in a public green site located within the infested zone, had been sprayed once in early spring and according to the technician in charge no further symptoms or actual presence of T. erytreae had been observed during the summer. However, the audit team identified a number of specimens of adults feeding on leaves and nymphs of different development stages on recently flushed foliage; In another case, the owner of an orchard with Citrus trees in a private garden had reported to the regional plant health services the possibility of T. erytreae presence in August 2015. Traps placed by the DRAP of the North region indicated that T. erytreae was present in the region and that the flight period reached its peak in June. Following the finding, the owner carried out severe pruning of the trees and applied insecticide treatments using a professional contractor for this purpose. Three treatments were carried out late June, mid-July and late August, which is too late to inhibit the early development of T. erytreae from nymphs to adults and overall suppress its population dynamics. The inspectors stated that it was not critically important to start applying early insecticide treatments in the centre of the infested zone, particularly whilst there are other factors governing when the plants can be treated: the continuous flowering of lemon trees (presence of bees) and the need to observe a withdrawal period before picking lemons. 5.3.4 Movement of susceptible material

The competent authority has elaborated control measures that should, if applied systematically, inhibit further spread of the pest in line with Article 16(1) of the same Directive. However, these measures are not systematically applied or their enforcement within the infested zone of the demarcated areas is not efficient and the pest continues to spread. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 16(1) of the same Directive 15 that all necessary measures must be taken to eradicate, or if that is impossible, inhibit the spread of the pest.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the audit process is subject to independent scrutiny as required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: IGAMAOT stated that the requirement for independent scrutiny of the audit process was a matter of internal concern and that they appreciated the opportunity provided by the DG SANTE audit to discuss the issue and to conduct an independent examination of IGAMAOT's audit process required by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. However, the DG SANTE audit team noted that there are no planned arrangements in place to ensure that this requirement is met on an on-going basis. The Network Reference Document on Independence and Independent Scrutiny (February 2014 - Version 1) defines the independent scrutiny as a "...regular and planned process...". The DG SANTE audit team consider that the DG SANTE audit provided independent scrutiny but is not sufficient to ensure on-going compliance with the requirement for independent scrutiny foreseen by Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Conclusions

No arrangements have been put in place by IGAMAOT to ensure independent scrutiny of the audit process. This means that it misses an opportunity to receive inputs for promoting continuous improvement of the audit process. 10 5.2.3 Auditor competence 5.2.3.1 Legal requirements Articles 2(6) and 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 do not lay down specific requirements regarding the competence of auditors. Article 6 of the same Regulation requires that staff performing official controls "receive, for their area of competence, appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently" and "keep up-to-date in their area of competence and receive regular additional training as necessary" Section 6.6 of the Annex of Commission Decision 2006/677 provides guidance on auditor competence: "Auditor competence and selection criteria should be defined under the following headings: -- generic knowledge and skills -- audit principles, procedures and techniques; management/organisational skills, -- specific technical knowledge and skills, -- personal attributes, -- education, -- work experience, -- auditor training and experience. It is essential to put a mechanism in place to ensure auditors are consistent and their competencies are maintained. Competencies required by audit teams will vary depending on the area they are auditing within the control or supervision systems. As regards the technical knowledge and skills required by auditors, the training requirements for staff performing official controls (Chapter 1 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 882/2004) should also be considered." 5.2.3.2 Findings

citations.text: The audit programme of DGAV foresees the coverage of all national control plans as defined in the MANCP to be audited at least once in the five-year cycle. There are 30 such areas and in some cases an audit can cover more than one area of activity (e.g. official import controls at the border inspection posts and the RASFF). The CCA commented that the multi-annual audit programme has considered the risk that each area represents. In addition, in the preparation of the annual audit programme the CCA considers the results of previous audits, emerging issues and requests from regional authorities, and adds a maximum of 10% to the total number of routine audits (so-called sporadic audits) for such areas. The CCA explained that the higher risk areas are audited more than once in the five-year cycle but this selection and the prioritisation over the lower risk areas is not documented. Therefore it cannot be demonstrated and justified why some thematic areas are selected for more frequent audits than others.

In 2013, IGAMAOT developed a comprehensive risk analysis methodology to be used in the preparation of the audit programme. This methodology was communicated to DGAV as a tool to be considered in the preparation of their audit programme. The audit team noted that this methodology has not been systematically used so far by either CCA.

The CCAs have properly defined certain audit areas (e.g. animal health controls are defined by different thematic areas, namely eradication and monitoring of tuberculosis and brucellosis in ruminants, bluetongue disease, transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, Salmonella control programmes in poultry, avian influenza, diseases of farmed fish, bee health, etc.). However, some other areas are not sufficiently detailed (e.g. the approval and control of establishments covers meat, meat products, and fish but is it not made clear how different types of meat are categorised based on the varying foodborne hazards inherent to each type and whether catering facilities, restaurants etc. are considered and/or covered). IGAMAOT provided during the audit an updated map (audit universe) of the areas of official controls.

The CCAs have arrangements in place audit programming and the effective coverage of the defined areas of official controls in the five-year audit cycle. However, the process for developing the audit programme is not well-documented or transparent and it is not clear as to the order of its risk-based prioritisation. The CCAs could not demonstrate the risk basis for deciding the frequency of auditing of specific areas.

citations.text: Although the DG SANTE audit focussed on these two main CAs based on the assessment of the audit arrangements for the coverage of the official controls in Portugal, the audit team requested clarifications as regards the extent to which Madeira implement Article 4(6), as no information was available during the audit. The competent authority in Madeira in a reply to an IGAMAOT email confirmed that no audit arrangements are in place to cover the official controls in that region. In this context, it is worth positively highlighting the Azores model, in which an agreement between the regional CA and DGAV is in place to ensure compliance with Article 4(6). The audit team noted that this is a useful model for dealing with the challenges of implementing Article 4(6) on small islands with autonomous regional CAs.

The multi-annual audit programme agreed between DGAV and IGAMAOT (see findings 3 and 4) does not cover the official controls in Madeira, for example, the border inspection posts and the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF). This means that the arrangements in place for the co-ordination to ensure a seamless audit process across the relevant competent authorities are not sufficient in the case of the audits on official controls in Madeira. IGAMAOT stated that its co-ordinating role covers the auditing of official control systems in the mainland of Portugal, but nevertheless, the Madeira CA is always invited to the co-ordination meetings but has attended only once. Conclusions

The absence of an audit system in Madeira means that the official controls in that region are not subject to a systematic and independent examination and there are no guarantees on the extent to which the official controls systems comply with the relevant EU legislation and meet the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 7

recommendations.text: Ensure that checks can be, and are, carried out on samples that are representative of the consignment from which they are taken, in line with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

citations.text: However, the DGAV informed the audit team that at another inspection point at Lisbon port the unloading bay at the place of inspection is too limited and that it is not possible to fully unload the consignment from containers. They have been in discussion with other official services to obtain access to the adequate place of inspection which would allow complete unloading of the containers. This is not specifically required by Directive 98/22/EC, although the absence of such facilities means that the DGAV in not in a position to ensure that checks can be carried on the entirety or a representative sample of consignments, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(ii) or (iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 12

The audit team noted that, with respect to sampling: The inspectors stated that during busy periods they take a sample to achieve 95% confidence level to detect 1% infestation level, otherwise they take a larger sample to achieve 99% confidence level to detect 1% infestation level in line with ISPM 31. In case of citrus fruits, inspectors confirmed that they apply a sample size of 200 fruits, based on the sample size required by Decision 2016/715, regardless of the origin of the lot being sampled. In the case of limes, imported from Columbia (two containers with 21 600 kg each), the inspector stated that four boxes were taken from the first two rows to compile the sample of 200 fruits. In this case the containers were not unloaded as it was not considered necessary because it was a mixed consignment of a regular trade from a known exporter with a good history of compliance. In the case of a mango consignment which consisted of 1 551 boxes (with 7 fruits per box), 64 boxes were taken to obtain a sample of 448 fruits for visual inspection (99% confidence level to detect 1% infestation level). The same approach was taken during the plant health checks of two other mango consignments. In all cases inspectors had access to the entire consignments of mango, but only took a sample for visual inspection from a single pallet, selected by the inspector. Inspectors stated that in the case of cut flowers consignment from Thailand (2 000 stems in 10 boxes) they selected five boxes and visually checked the entire content of each box.

The DGAV stated that concerning the representativeness of the sample, the inspection guide and instructions provide that samples should be taken from different parts of the consignment. Similarly, for containerised consignments, containers should be fully unloaded to allow proper inspection. However, the inspections observed by the audit team and interviews with inspectors confirmed that this was not always implemented. In addition to that, as noted in section 5.4.1 above, there was a lack of proper inspection facilities at one inspection post at Lisbon port which prevented access to consignments 14 in containers. The sample size is adequate, however, in certain cases, it could not be fully ensured that the sample was actually representative of the consignment, as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

The import checks in Portugal are carried out meticulously, in line with EU legislation. However, due to the lack of facilities at one inspection post and the practice of taking all the samples from a single part of the consignment, in some cases the representativeness of the samples is not ensured.

citations.text: Based on data provided by the ICNF, the audit team estimated that overall, one FTE was responsible for the survey and monitoring of more than 100,000 ha. The ICNF staff involved in these tasks confirmed the difficulty in doing everything in a timely manner in such a big area, especially for those who were also responsible for other tasks. The audit team indeed noted that despite the motivation of staff, they had difficulty to keep up with all their tasks in the territory they were responsible for (see section 5.4). 5.1.4 Laboratories

The system is undermined by human resources available which are too limited to ensure that all PWN-related control measures are implemented throughout the buffer zone in accordance with the national plan or guidance (see sections 5.2.3 and 5.4).

In the two Regions visited, the regional service of the ICNF informed that the territory of the buffer zone had been divided up and allocated to different teams of one or two staff members. They stated that all the territorial units were visited at least once a year and that a number of them were visited more than once (see also section 5.2.2). Although their objectives was to identify as many trees dead or in decline in Autumn- Winter with a view to "clean" the buffer zone before the start of the flight season, the ICNF staff stated that it was not possible to visit all the territorial units during this period. After the Summer of 2016, allocation of resources had been increased in areas affected by fire in the district of Viana do Castelo and those affected by drought and close to the infested zone in the district of Castelo Branco. This had been done by shifting resources within Regions and requesting support from the central service of the ICNF.

The audit team noted that the FITO system did not cater for recording monitoring activities except when trees were identified and sampled. Several ICNF staff members involved in the monitoring stated that they had been working in the forest area and/or in the same Region for many years and did not need such a tool to make sure that all parts of the buffer zone under their responsibility had been monitored. Some of them were using printed maps to mark those territorial units monitored over a certain period. The ICNF informed the audit team that work had been initiated in order to adapt the national recording system FITO so that field teams could record their monitoring activities and the central service is able to monitor progress made and confirm that the entire buffer zone is monitored in a comprehensive and timely way. 15

The audit team visited the buffer zone in two Regions and noted that forest areas were in good condition, with the exception of areas affected by fire in the Region North. The audit team noted the presence of some declining trees in different locations. In a number of these locations, these trees had already been identified and sampled. In some other locations, only a portion of the trees had been identified and the ICNF stated that the additional trees would be identified (i.e. recorded in FITO) and sampled at felling. In other locations, dead or declining trees had not been identified and sampled although, in some cases, the ICNF staff stated that they were aware of their presence but had had no time to sample and record them in FITO. The audit team noted that many of the unidentified trees had started declining in the past few months.

The identification of trees dead or in decline and their sampling is largely performed in accordance with point 3(a) of Annex II of Decision 2012/535/EU. However, the fact that human resources are not sufficient to allow the identification, recording and sampling of all dead or declining trees 1) to always be done as soon as they are noticed by the staff involved and 2) throughout the buffer zone during the Autumn-Winter, prevents the timely elimination of these trees and therefore lead to a risk of PWN spreading into the buffer zone.

recommendations.text: When drafting the residue monitoring plan to broaden the scope of analysis for subgroup B1 substances as to ensure that samples can be selected based on the criteria mentioned in point 2.3.3.1. of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC.

citations.text: BACKGROUND The 2011 audit identified that the implementation of the residue monitoring plans of 2010 and 2011 was insufficient due to budgetary problems, causing delays to analyse samples taken and consequently limited the effectiveness of follow-up activities in the event of non-compliant results. The reliability of analytical results was also undermined as not all of the methods used for testing samples under the plan were validated. The legal requirements to permit slaughter of horses only on the basis of food chain information contained in the horse passport had not always been respected.

recommendations.text: CAs should improve the performance of inspectors involved in official controls of FCM by providing them with the relevant tools (i.e. training and technical support) in order to give effect to the requirement set out in Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 regarding FCM safety and, thus, to ensure effective and appropriate official controls as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004.

citations.text: At the first FCM manufacturer (producer of PET bottles) the inspectors verified the DoC of the ready-to-use bottle, asked questions regarding the raw materials used, identified an issue with regard to surface/volume ratio and also requested to see the supporting documents. The inspectors confirmed that they were not able to go further on what is already stated in the DoC since more expertise is needed. 13

The second FCM manufacturer (PET bottles blower) was inspected for the first time in relation to FCM. DoCs concerning raw materials and final products were requested and evaluated by the inspectors. However no further supporting documentation was requested and the inspectors did not ask for the risk assessment performed by the BO concerning the blowing procedure in order to evaluate the effect of the process.

At the third manufacturer, the inspectors carried out a verification check in relation to FCM (see paragraph 31). The inspectors examined additional documents provided and decided for which areas action was still required by the BO. They stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the completeness of the DoC and the supporting documentation. They informed the audit team that they can only evaluate what the BO provides to them. If a substance is not mentioned in the DoC they do not have the expertise to find out if such a substance is not present in the formula or is not mentioned for whatever reason.

The audit team observed that inspectors rely mainly on what the BOs provide to them during the inspections concerning manufacturing procedures and risk analysis including the presence of non-intentionally added substances (NIAS). The inspectors have limited expertise to evaluate the formula for a product or to identify if information concerning certain substances is missing. There was no documentary evidence that they systematically requested organoleptic test results from BOs.

The audit team noted that official controls on plastics, in most cases, do not include sufficient checks on the supporting documentation for statements in the DoC (final product). In particular, the following were missing: An assessment of the supporting documentation relating to the completeness of laboratory results in matters of SML or organoleptic tests; An assessment of NIAS ­ e.g. impurities, reaction products and decomposition that can occur during the processing of a granulate into the final product; A verification of the BO's risk assessment required under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) No 10/2011.

At one DRAP visited the audit team noted that the evaluation of DoCs covers the formal aspects. The inspectors stated that they do not have the expertise to evaluate the formula of the product and thus they are not able to determine if a substance is not present in a product or if the DoC is incomplete. In a particular case, and although the DoC was forwarded to the NRL and DGAV for their opinion on whether to carry out sampling, neither provided feedback advising DRAP's inspectors that the specific DoC was incomplete (substance missing), since they also rely completely on the information provided by the BO.

The CCA informed the audit team that the risk assessments carried out by FCM manufacturers and/or processors, for substances referred to in Article 19 of Regulation 14 (EU) No 10/2011 had to date not been requested and therefore not evaluated by the inspectors since that requires specific knowledge and expertise and support from central level. However, such a support was not available (and it had never been sought) at the time of the audit.

Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points (HACCP) plans are evaluated by the inspectors also in relation to the chemical hazards associated with FCM used. However, concerning FCM, the inspectors during the documentary checks relied on the information provided by the FBO rather than checking whether chemical risks associated with FCM foreseeable use are adequately identified and managed by the FBO2. 2 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that relevant questions of this topic can be raised during the visit to the facilities. 15

Regarding this specific case the audit team requested that the inspectors sought an expert opinion. Based on the information they collected on-the-spot a draft expert opinion was prepared by central level identifying certain non-compliances related to the articles/ FCM selected. Some non-compliances not related to the DoCs had not be identified by the inspectors during their control but were mentioned in the expert opinion. The expert opinion drafted contained information on what the inspectors should additionally request of the FCM retailer to be able to conclude whether the article/FCM in question complied with the legal requirements.

ASAE informed the audit team that FCM controls were not a priority at the time of the audit and therefore advice/guidance from central level was rarely sought. It was explained that in 2016, and although a few non-compliances were identified related to the DoC, the possibility of requesting an expert opinion was not availed of.

The audit team examined a case of such a documentary check and saw that the relevant information DoC and supporting documents were attached to the file. The analysis mentioned on supporting documents related to ceramic material whereas the actual import concerned a plastic material. This was not identified by the inspectors during the import control.

During official controls inspectors are able to verify the presence of DoC and, to a certain extent, to assess the completeness of those declarations. Limited controls were made on the completeness of supporting documentation for the DoC, which would lead to inadequate or incomplete risk assessments/DoCs being overlooked. Thus, non- compliant products might go undetected and correct application of the relevant legislation would not be enforced.

The effectiveness of the controls in place is hampered by the fact that inspectors are not suitably trained or experienced to evaluate compliance of FCM legislation, including a thorough analysis of the DoC and supporting documentation. Expertise available at central level is rarely sought3. 3 In their response to the draft report the CCA noted that concerning two DRAPs visited, whenever doubts are raised, an official request for support is sent to the Directorate-General for Food and Veterinary Matters - Department for Nutrition and Food. Different situations may result from the fact that the level of knowledge differentiation among the technicians carrying out the checks is still such that they are not able to determine the relevance of any questions that should perhaps be raised. 17 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures and Laboratory Performances Legal Requirements Article 4(2)(c), Article 11, Article 12(1), (2) and (3) and Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. citations.text: In every establishment visited, the audit team checked the DSAVR feed inspectors' assessment of operators' hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans. In a few cases, the inspectors' assessment was sufficient. However, in eight of the 11 establishments visited, the audit team noted shortcomings in relation to the adequacy of operators' risk assessment for some ingredients used for the production of feed additives, and for some of the feed additives themselves (predominantly contaminants of chemical origin, e.g., heavy metals, dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), lack of information on bacterial strain used for production of certain additives, etc.). The failure 5 of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had been identified in any of the previous inspection reports. In one operator, there was no adequate HACCP plan in place at the time of the visit. (6)

The new inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by under-implementation, deficient assessment of operators' HACCP-plans and incomplete verification of the appropriateness of operators' retained samples. recommendations.text: To ensure that staff carrying out official sampling, laboratories performing analytical testing and staff interpreting the analytical results, follow the requirements laid down by Article 1 and Annex I and II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

citations.text: A systemic shortcoming was noted by the audit team in terms of the preparation of final samples from the aggregate samples for control of substances where non-uniform distribution of the analyte/substance is presumed. The inspectors would normally use simple manual mixing to ensure appropriate homogenisation rather than special equipment (e.g., mechanical or automatic dividers) which is required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with a non-uniform distribution, simple manual mixing alone cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample. The DAA informed the audit team that mechanical dividers are not available for the DSAVR inspectors, but the third party designated for sampling in certain cases (albeit very minor proportion of the official samples; see finding 39) do have the necessary equipment.

The audit team examined a number of laboratory reports and noted that not all of the parameters (i.e. expanded measurement uncertainty, correction for recovery and moisture content), necessary for interpretation of the results in accordance with the requirements laid down by part C(6) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009, had been reported and thus could not been taken into account by the DAA when making its decision on compliance. In addition, the laboratory reports seen did not provide an unambiguous statement that the number of analytical determinations for non-compliant results had been in accordance with the requirements laid down by part C(3) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling

The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of this element of official controls is weakened by the competent authorities' failure to adhere to planned arrangements and by the fact that the representativeness of sampling, and thus samples' legal and analytical validity, is not ensured for substances with a non-uniform distribution.

The interpretation of the analytical results does not take into account all required parameters thus weakening the legal validity of the decisions made by the competent authority on compliance. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

citations.text: In every region visited, the audit team studied a number of non-compliances from previous controls (DGAV's area of responsibility). Examples included deficient labelling, HACCP-related deficiencies, and non-compliant sampling results. While follow-up of deficient labelling and HACCP-related deficiencies was largely adequate and effective, the audit team noted that, for non-compliant results on carry-over and exceeding maximum permitted levels for certain trace elements, the communication with the FeBOs had not contained an unambiguous request for corrective action and consequently no timeframe had been specified for the FeBO to remedy the deficiency(ies). Dedicated and comprehensive follow-ups were not properly carried out by the competent authority. No attempts had been made to ensure that the relevant FeBOs identified the reason(s) for the non-compliances and thus ensured that the issues would not recur. The situation observed is not in line with the requirements laid down by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that there was reasonably detailed and adequate guidance on how to deal with non-compliances and the relevant actions to take ­ but only for Salmonella, processed animal proteins and forbidden substances (as per Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 767/2009). Conclusion on the actions taken on non-compliances

The fact that the competent authority (DGAV) does not ensure that the operators identify the reason(s) for all non-compliances identified and remedy those weakens the effectiveness of the overall control system. 5.2.4 Establishments producing/trading non-authorised (in the EU) feed additives and exporting or re-exporting them from the EU to a third country

recommendations.text: The competent authority should make additional provisions for pig producers to correctly identify all relevant risk factors for tail biting in order that they can ensure that those animals are not caused any unnecessary pain, suffering or injury, as required by Article 3 of Directive 98/58/EC. and audit findings in Annex 2.

citations.text: The audit team saw two paper questionnaire draft replies (not yet sent to the official services) and several online replies. The producers had marked a number of parameters as 'not being a risk factor' although they had no available data and/or they should clearly have identified them as risk factors. For example, after replying that they had no measurements of relative humidity, gas (CO2 or NH3) concentrations, and/or active ventilation systems (with temperatures in summer frequently exceeding 30°C) none of these was considered a risk factor. The only factor that producers were almost 7 unanimously considering a risk factor was the quality and amount of enrichment material. This, together with registering tail biting were the only areas for improvement included in the holdings' action plans that the audit team saw. Pig sector associations

There is a defined level of tail biting below which pig producers will have to start rearing some batches of pigs with full tails. However, the fact that producers are not yet correctly identifying all risk factors for tail biting is likely to cause significant delays in rearing the first batches of full tail pigs or to result in major tail biting outbreaks in those batches.

The audit team asked why those were the only risk factors identified for improvement. Both producers indicated that those were the only two parameters (chains not being adequate as enrichment material, and lack of registers of tail biting) for which they were not in compliance with mandatory criteria.

Temperatures inside the houses were 35°C and higher (with only a few animals in a few pens showing signs of discomfort, panting), and a number of pigs were concentrated around the bowl drinker in most pens and episodically competed for access to it. Both producers considered these conditions normal and did not identify them in their draft risk assessment as areas for improvement (see also paragraph 29).

Both producers dealt with tail biting outbreaks in similar ways by using management measures such as identifying and separating the biter(s) and/or treating the tails of bitten animals with drying agents. However, they kept using the same enrichment material of only marginal interest, chains, or other marginal or suboptimal materials such as plastic toys.

responses.response: The DGAV will seek, in collaboration with the FPAS (Portuguese g in Federation of Pig's Association) and the "Sociedade Científica de Suinicultura" (Scientific Society of Pig Farming), to promote clarification sessions on the theme of tail-docking and management of pig farms. The training curricula of pig farmers will be reviewed within the framework of Animal Welfare, with the aim of consolidating the knowledge on risk factors of tail docking and their prevention. We will seek to strengthen the need to implement the requirements regarding the competence, experience and training of the pigs' holders, with the FPAS and the "Sociedade Cientifica de Suinicultura" (Scientific Society of Pig Farming). The dissemination of the material prepared by the DGAV will be reinforced, within the scope of the reduction of tail-docking, prevention of tail docking and the use of manipulable materials.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that official controls correctly report routine tail docking as non-compliance, in line with the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC; so that this is also correctly reported under Commission Decision 2006/778/EC.

citations.text: Until 2019, the official control reports indicated that routine tail docking was performed but reported this as compliant despite lack of evidence at holdings of injuries to sows' teats or to other pigs' ears and tails, which is not in line with the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of the Pig Directive. 10

DGAV updated the manual of procedures for official controls, and relevant associated instructions, in March 2019 (see also Annex 2). They included additional considerations for the official controls to determine if tail docking is to be considered non-compliance by referring to the two recently added compliance criteria, i.e. if the producer does not keep registers of tail biting or does not have an action plan with improvement measures then this should be considered non-compliant.

Official controls correctly detect routine tail docking but they report it as being compliant. This causes under reporting of non-compliances in pig farms in the annual report to the Commission (in connection with Commission Decision 2006/778/EC).

responses.response: The Animal Welfare Control Manual, used as a basis for official controls, will be revised with a view to reinforcing the need to register and consider non-compliant tail docking practice in line th the legislation (lack of tail docking records that justify tail docking and failure to take action on identified risk factors). In September/October 2019, targeted training actions for the technical staff of the Regional Directorates for Food and Veterinary (DSAVR) (training actions in different regions) are planned regarding the action plan for tail docking in pigs, where the need to improve the assessment of compliance with the legislation in this area will be reinforced.
