recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that official controls correctly indicate as non-compliance; enrichment material such as chains, insufficient to fulfil the essential needs for proper investigation and manipulation, in line with point 4 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and Commissio (EU) 2016/336; and routine tail docking, in line with the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of Council Directive 2008/120/EC; in order for official controls to require operators to take corrective action, in line with Article 8, 3, (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council. and audit findings in Annex 2.

citations.text: Until 2019, the official control reports indicated that routine tail docking was performed but reported this as compliant despite lack of evidence at holdings of injuries to sows' teats or to other pigs' ears and tails, which is not in line with the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of the Pig Directive. 10

The most recent official controls (in 2014 to one holding and 2018 to the other) did not report any non-compliance in either of these holdings. The only enrichment material present was chains (identified in the Commission Recommendation (EU) 2016/336 and accompanying Staff Working Document as insufficient to fulfil the essential needs) which, similarly to the absence of registers of tail biting, the producers had recently identified as an area for improvement.

In both holdings animals were in satisfactory conditions and, other than the lack of adequate enrichment material, the audit team did not observe any serious non- compliance with general rearing conditions.

Both producers dealt with tail biting outbreaks in similar ways by using management measures such as identifying and separating the biter(s) and/or treating the tails of bitten animals with drying agents. However, they kept using the same enrichment material of only marginal interest, chains, or other marginal or suboptimal materials such as plastic toys.

Official controls correctly detect routine tail docking but they report it as being compliant. This causes under reporting of non-compliances in pig farms in the annual report to the Commission (in connection with Commission Decision 2006/778/EC).

The new reference criteria have only been recently added to the official controls instructions and verification of their implementation has not started yet. The narrow scope of compliance criteria will prevent inspectors from fully enforcing these 13 requirements.

responses.response: The Animal Welfare Control Manual, used as a basis for official controls, will be revised with the aim of reinforcing the need to consider as non-compliant the exclusive use of chains, as well as routine tail-docking without complying with legal requirements. September/October 2019, targeted training is planned for the DSAVR technical staff (training actions in the different regions) regarding the action plan for tail docking in pigs, where the need to improve the assessment of compliance with the legislation and ction, the assessment of manipulable material will be reinforced. Within the scope of cross-compliance controls, from 2020 onwards, it is intended that the legal criteria regarding the practice of routine tail-docking and the use of manipulable materials are assessed in more detail and taking into account the Action Plan, the answers to the producers' questionnaires, as well as the good practices established and widely disseminated. This matter will be discussed with the local veterinary services at the next follow-up meeting of the Action Plan.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should provide additional compliance criteria so that farmers have a clear indication of what is required and official controls can more effectively enforce the legal requirements of Council Directive 2008/120/EC and Council Directive 98/58/EC that are related to risk factors for tail biti and audit findings in Annex 2.

citations.text: In March 2019 DGAV established criteria (see also paragraphs 16 and 17) in the updated manual of procedures for official controls that correctly include a combination of both resource-based values and animal-based indicators as required in the Commission Recommendation (EU) 2016/336. Compliance criteria now added are that pig producers must keep records of tail biting and attempt improvement measures. Other added criteria are guidance instead of compliance criteria other than for those explicitly described in the Pig Directive such as slat width, stocking density where a specific value or measure is stated. Guidance criteria, values and indicators include: access to water and feed where it indicates a minimum number of drinkers, and minimum length of feeders available per animal and additionally indicates that the animals must have 'easy access'; gas and dust concentrations/presence where it provides maximum values that official controls should measure and additionally indicates some signs in the animals (i.e. inflammation of the eyes or respective mucosa and/or breathing problems) of the excessive presence of those gases and dust.

In adopting guidance criteria, referenced in paragraph 12, Portugal has failed to define the necessary level of compliance criteria to enable official controls and the pig sector to make an assessment of compliance with the legal requirements of the Pig Directive and of Directive 98/58/EC. Action plan

The competent authorities together with producers, veterinarians and scientific support produced comprehensive guidance and monitoring tools. The authorities will have difficulties to enforce existing legislative requirements related to risk factors as the new criteria they set are mainly guidance instead of compliance criteria.

Portugal's adoption of mainly guidance instead of compliance criteria (see also paragraph 12) for the requirement s of the second paragraph of point 8 of Chapter I of Annex I of the Pig Directive on the avoidance of routine tail docking prevent it from fully complying with its obligations under EU law. The authorities do not regard producers who do not respect the values for the guidance criteria added to the official instructions (such as easy access to feed and water, thermal comfort, sufficient air renewal, gas concentrations, sufficient enrichment material) as non-compliant.

However, Article 2(b) of Commission Recommendation (EU) 336/2016 restates the obligation of Member States to establish compliance criteria with the requirements set out in the legislation. Such mandatory criteria are necessary for official controls to be able to enforce the legislative requirements effectively.

The audit team asked why those were the only risk factors identified for improvement. Both producers indicated that those were the only two parameters (chains not being adequate as enrichment material, and lack of registers of tail biting) for which they were not in compliance with mandatory criteria.

The new reference criteria have only been recently added to the official controls instructions and verification of their implementation has not started yet. The narrow scope of compliance criteria will prevent inspectors from fully enforcing these 13 requirements.

Instructions for official controls under those new requirements are adequate. However the producers' lack of recognition and acceptance of several stress factors present for tail biting, combined with most additional criteria being only guidance, may cause major delays, or even refusal, from producers to act on official controls' indications of areas they should improve.

responses.response: The Animal Welfare Control Manual, used as a basis for official controls, will be revised, seeking to improve the way legal requirements are assessed (linked to risk factors for tail docking) d the indicators to determine their non-compliance (animal and resource based indicators). Instructions to producers will be drawn up on the basis of the criteria to be reviewed in the context of controls and found to be non-compliant. Page: 2

recommendations.text: To ensure that the classification of production areas, the monitoring of production areas for microbiological quality and for biotoxins and the decisions taken following the microbiological monitoring are carried out in line with Articles 54.2 and 3, 57, 61 62 and 63 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. (a)(b) and (d).

citations.text: The classification of production, included in the IPMA procedure MB 01, foresees three types of classification: permanent, provisional and not classified, depending on the number of results available during the review period. The audit team noted that: For provisional classification, a reduced number of sampling results (between 12 and 23) in three years is sufficient for IPMA to classify provisionally a specific species in a production area with a better class than other species in the same area. The audit team considered that less than 24 results in three years does not ensure that results are representative of a production area, as required in Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Nonetheless, IPMA could use those results for the initial classification if twelve of them are obtained within six months, as foreseen in the mentioned guidance document of the European Union Reference Laboratory (EURL) for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs10. According to the procedure, IPMA should not classify a production area if there are less than twelve sampling results for a given species in less than three years. However, this is not implemented and IPMA classifies all species existing in an area with the less favourable permanent classification given to the area. In principle, there are no negative implications with this practice but it is not in line with its own procedure. 5.1.2 Monitoring of classified production areas

According to the procedure MB 02, laboratory reports have to include the Most Probable Result (MPR) of E. coli per 100 grams. However, the number of dilutions made during the analyses of samples from class B production areas is not enough to provide an exact number when results are > 18,000. Therefore, it is not possible to determine if these areas exceed the limit of 46,000 established in Article 54.3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for class B production, and decisions for reclassification and/or closure of production areas cannot be adequately taken. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

According to the procedure MB 03, and in line with Article 61.4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, the indicator species shall be sampled on a weekly basis (other species only when testing of indicator species result is over the limits for biotoxins). However, for different reasons (e g. indicator species not available, weather conditions, etc.) IPMA does not always respect this frequency. IPMA does not always take the samples at the points designated in the procedure according to Article 61.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Indicator species are sometimes sampled in other locations or other species are sampled instead and used as indicator.

The decisions following results over the limits are included in the procedure MB 01, but it has a number of deviations from the legislation: a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs The procedure does not foresee the closure or reclassification of production areas when health standards for live bivalve molluscs are not met (i.e. between 230 and 700 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas, between 4,600 and 46,000 E. coli NMP/100 g for class B production areas), contrary to Article 62.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. IPMA reclassifies production areas when monitoring results are >700 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas and closes production areas when monitoring results are >46,000 E. coli NMP/100 g for all classes of production areas. It carries out an investigation to determine the possible reasons for the unexpected result. The audit team reviewed the two cases and noted that the outcome of the investigation was not conclusive. Despite this, IPMA considered these results as anomalous and therefore excluded from the data set considered during the review period for classification. b) A downgrade in classification when results are exceeded is reverted following two good results within the expected limits (i.e. 230 E. coli NMP/100 g for class A production areas, 4,600 E. coli NMP/100 g for class B production areas) separated 15 days. This reversion should only take place if the evaluation of the results available for the review period determine compliance with the corresponding standards, as established in line with Article 52 .3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. c) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water The audit team noted that, except in one case, IPMA always followed the procedure. Exceeding prohibition limits triggered the preventive closure of production areas for all species of molluscs as required by Article 62.1of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. d) For the presence of biotoxins in live bivalve molluscs The audit team noted that IPMA only closes preventively production areas due to a lack of samples available when samples are not available for more than 2 12 In their response to the draft report IPMA confirmed that they could not use reference material of bivalve matrix because it was not available on the market. 9 weeks. This is not in line with Article 61.4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 that requires weekly testing for biotoxins. e) For the presence of chemical contaminants in live bivalve molluscs The audit team saw several examples of classified production areas closed due to exceeding levels of heavy metals.

As, in general, the classification of production areas is consistent with the EU classification requirements and supported by recommendations from sanitary surveys, there is confidence that the level of contamination of molluscs harvested corresponds to the value expected according to their classification. The provisional classification based on a reduced number of results may overestimate the microbiological quality of mollusc.

The few cases where the results of the microbiological monitoring of class B production areas do not provide an exact result (number) pose a challenge to the decisions for reclassification and/or closure of these production areas.

The fact that IPMA: i) does not close or reclassify the production area when certain regulatory limits for microbiological quality are exceeded; ii) reverts the classification downgrade without an evaluation of the results for the review period; iii) excludes unexpected results without conclusive investigation, may result in the placing on the market of bivalve molluscs that exceed the health standards.

The current monitoring programme for biotoxins covers most of the requirements of EU legislation but the fact that the IPMA does not fully respect the sampling points and frequencies diminishes its value.

responses.response: Review of the IPMA, I.P./SNMB procedure MB01 in line with Articles ons 54.2 and 3, 57, 61 62 and 63 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 Review proposal of next classification accordingly. Until end of 2nd 2021 semester.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the training and supervision of non-official samplers when sampling classified production areas for monitoring according to Article 59 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, provide enough guarantee that the sampling is reliable.

citations.text: IPMA analyses all monitoring samples in its laboratories and there is a dedicated budget line to pay for these analyses. IPMA staff take monitoring samples, but also individual harvesters, harvesters' associations or aquaculture production companies with a contract with IPMA (there is no financial compensation for the sampling activities or for the samples themselves). Since 2015, IPMA has enhanced the content of contracts for 10 The guidance document of the EU Reference Laboratory for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs ("Good Practice Guide; issue 7", December 2018). 5 sampling to make them more comprehensive, to include a training session from IPMA staff to samplers and a manual with the requirements for the adequate collection of samples. In the last years, IPMA started to supervise these samplers; since the beginning of 2020, its objective is to supervise 35% of them every year. IPMA confirmed its intention to formalise all this in a procedure. Although the use of non-official staff for monitoring sampling is not explicitly foreseen in EU legislation, Article 65.2 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, allows competent authorities to take into account the results of checks carried out by food business operators or organisations representing food business operators when deciding on the classification, reclassification, opening or closure of production areas. This is possible provided that: the laboratory carrying out the analysis is designated by the competent authorities, and the sampling and analysis are performed in accordance with a protocol agreed upon jointly by the competent authorities and food business operators or organisation concerned. In addition, Article 30 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 establishes the conditions for delegating certain official control tasks to natural persons. Therefore, although not foreseen as such in EU legislation, this type of sampling should not, in principle, be a problem because sampling is performed in accordance with a protocol agreed upon jointly and because IPMA has arrangements in place to verify the reliability of the sampling, avoiding in this way any possible impartiality or conflict of interest by the samplers. a) For microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs

The IPMA's intention to formalise the procedure for sampling of classified production areas by non-official staff is essential to ensure that samples taken in the context of official monitoring are reliable.

responses.response: IPMA, I.P./SNMB will write a new procedure to reflect the current f practice on training and supervision of official and non-official samplers. Concluded (Annex 1)

recommendations.text: To ensure that analytical method used for classification and for microbiological monitoring of production areas, required respectively by Articles 52 and 59 (b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, provides reliable analytical results; and that the analytical method to detect lipophilic toxins comply with the requirements of Chapter III.B of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627 in all the cases.

citations.text: According to the procedure MB 02, monitoring samples have to be analysed using a method recognised by the National Reference Laboratory that should preferably be standardised. The audit team saw that the analyses of a certain number of samples from two production areas (they are remoter therefore more difficult to transport the samples on time) deviated from the method accredited and their analyses started more than 24 hours after collection. Accordingly, laboratory reports do not display the accreditation logo. However, IPMA used these results for classification and for decisions following monitoring. IPMA informed the audit team of an ongoing project to estimate the difference in results when analyses start more than 24 hours after the collection of samples; subsequently IPMA will consider an amendment in the scope of the 6 laboratory's accreditation to bring this in line with Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/62511.

The results of microbiological analysis using non-accredited testing methods are not 11 reliable and thus they generate the risk of misclassification of the areas. However, this risk is limited to only some of the monitoring samples of two of the 39 classified production areas.

The head of the biotoxins laboratories presented the facilities and equipment of the laboratories. The facilities of the three laboratories are appropriate. The equipment of the ASP and PSP laboratories is also adequate. There was only one piece of equipment validated for lipophilic toxins. In case of breakdown or regular maintenance (which is regularly required for this type of equipment), samples were analysed using a screening test which does not comply with the requirements of Chapter III.B of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In addition, this test only detects two of the regulated compounds (OA and DTX) so the total toxicity of the lipophilic toxin group can be underestimated.

Although the IPMA laboratory for lipophilic toxins routinely uses the EU analytical reference method to determine these toxins, the use of a non-recognised method on certain occasions means that the result in this biotoxin group, could be sporadically 15 non-reliable or underestimated.

responses.response: cal IPMA, I.P. is making a statistical study on the influence of time in b) sample results to prove that arrival later 24h up 36h does not affect he results. Until end of 2nd 2021 semester. Acquisition and validation of LC-MS/MS equipment, to reinforce the analytical capacity of the Biotoxins Lab. Until end of 1st 2022 semester.

recommendations.text: To ensure that there is a competent authority with responsibilities to withdraw from the market molluscs that can pose a risk for consumers, in line with Article 14 of Regulation (EU) No 178/2002, and to carry out official controls of marine gastropods harvested outside classified production areas, as required by Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624.

citations.text: The decisions taken by IPMA following results over the limits apply only from the moment when they are formalised (e.g. some days after the sample was taken). Similarly to the previous audit, the audit team noted that Portugal has not designated an authority responsible for withdrawing from the market those bivalve molluscs harvested between the day when the sample was taken and the day when the results are available. In the worst-case scenario, this period can be up to three days. As an example, the audit team noted one case where wedge clams were harvested in a production area closed on the same day due to lipophilic toxins. These clams, destined to another Member State, were sampled at the wholesaler of destination and resulted over the limits for Okadaic acid (which triggered a RASFF notification). 5.1.4 Recording and exchange of information

The exchange of information between the two competent authorities audited has clearly improved since the previous audit. IPMA presented evidence of regular and ad-hoc meetings with DGRMA and with other authorities. However, a significant lack of cooperation seems to persist in relation to the investigations derived from RASFFs notifications when they relate to health standards (i.e. microbiology and biotoxins). According to IPMA, except in one case, the contact point for RASFF (i.e. the DGAV) has never informed them of any notification or request any further investigation/explanation from them. This is not the case for RASFF notifications related to traceability: DGRM stated that DGAV referred to its services all notifications related to irregularities in the registration documents and, since the beginning of 2020, DGRM began to receive RASFF notifications directly. 10 5.1.5 Official controls of certain bivalve molluscs harvested outside classified production areas

Marine gastropods (except limpets) for human consumption, which can be harvested outside classified production areas, are not subject to the official controls required by Article 11 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624. At the time of the audit, Portugal has not designated an authority responsible for these controls. 5.1.6 Movement of live bivalve molluscs and registration document accompanying batches

The flow of information regarding monitoring results and the prompt update of available information helps the system to avoid mistakes due to delays. However, the current improvable cooperation between authorities and the absence of designated authorities for some parts of the food chain create the risk of molluscs that could pose a risk for consumers reaching and staying on the market.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the harvesting of live bivalve molluscs in closed classified production areas is prevented, as required in Article 62.1 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: The audit team reviewed two registration documents issued by harvesters with a license to harvest Japanese clams in a classified production areas in the Sado Estuary. In this estuary, the maximum daily limit of gathering per harvester is not regulated, whereas it is in others, e.g. in the Tagus Estuary, where there is a daily limit of 80 kg per harvester and the harvester has to use the fishing gear authorised for the purpose. In the Sado Estuary: there are two production areas with Japanese clams (among other molluscs species): one is classified as B and the other as forbidden due to very high levels of faecal contamination (>46,000 E. coli/100 g). The audit team review two registration documents, indicating 1,500 and 3,516 kg respectively. The audit team considers it physically impossible for a single person to harvest those amounts within a day. Conclusions on official controls on bivalve molluscs

There are indications that Japanese clams harvested in forbidden areas regularly reach the market. The current design and implementation of official control on licensed harvesters and registration documents facilitates quantities of molluscs much higher than those physically possible to catch and molluscs from forbidden areas reaching the market.

responses.response: IPMA sent letters to the potential Competent Authorities that may be appointed to deal with preventing harvesting of LBM in closed classified production areas. PM & GNR-UCM (Annex 3)

recommendations.text: Ensure that the surveillance carried out for the identification of dead or declining trees in the buffer zone will be increased and dead or declining trees identified during the flight season of the vector will be immediately felled and destroyed as required by point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II to Decision 2012/535/EU. 0

citations.text: Forest rangers follow a surveillance method based on a 100 ha grid of coordinates established throughout the buffer zone and its adjacent area for the identification of dead trees and trees in decline. They visit stands with high density of trees and stands found whilst crossing towards the targeted areas. As the areas to be monitored are not homogenous, the effectiveness of the surveys depends on the density of the stands with trees to be inspected. Additional work is planned and carried out in areas with dense pine forest, areas with dead and declining trees and high risk areas. The multi-annual action 9 plan provides for at least two visual surveys for spotting trees in decline throughout the year, in particular for plots located in high risk areas. Although this is considered a continuous action, surveys are mainly carried out after the summer, with some areas in close proximity or adjacent to the buffer zone not surveyed at a frequency, which would allow the earliest possible identification of declining trees (see also section 5.3 below). The ICNF stated that given the large size of the area in question (ca. 3.1 million hectares and 34 458 operational plots within the grid of coordinates), an extensive and continuous monitoring throughout the area, based on human resources, is obviously not permanent and that surveys are focusing on the autumn-winter season where the expression of declining symptoms on trees is high. The ICNF also stated that in collaboration with research and development entities are investigating the possibility for carrying out surveillance remotely.

Annual surveys are carried out according to the multi annual action plan elaborated by the CAs for the control of the PWN. The increased number of samples taken, particularly when sampling in the crown and placing traps and baits whilst targeting high risk areas, provide additional assurance with respect to the stated absence of the PWN from the buffer zone. However, a substantial part of the activities of the forest rangers is allocated to tasks other than surveillance for trees showing early declining symptoms. This reduces the likelihood of the earliest possible detection of PWN spread in the buffer zone, particularly during the summer.9

During its visits in different areas within the buffer zone the audit team spotted isolated trees and/or stands of dead trees and trees in decline, which were not affected by fire or storm. Some of these had already been recorded in FITO and marked to be felled by the private owners, whilst others were not. The ICNF stated that these trees had only recently started declining and that in any case, felling and removal operations could only take place in winter after signing a new contract with the felling operators. The ICNF also stated that due to the prohibition of movement of machinery for felling trees in the forest areas during the summer period when the probability of forest fires is high, they have extended the deadline for felling dead and declining trees in the winter until the end of March 2022. This was also the case in previous campaigns as there was high risk of forest fires during the summer. The non-marked trees were subsequently recorded in FITO for felling and sampling. 16

This approach results in dead and/or declining trees still standing after the end of the flight period of the vector in the summer, increasing the risk of PWN spread in the buffer zone. This is not in line with the first paragraph of point 3(b)(ii) of Annex II to Decision 2012/535/EU providing for the immediate felling and destruction of dead or declining trees identified on site. Instead, the ICNF systematically implements the provisions of the second paragraph of the same point to dead or declining trees in the buffer zone, which exclusively concerns trees affected by fire or storm. In any case, the risk of PWN spread is mitigated by the fact that PWN has not been detected so far in the buffer zone and by the fact that the incidents of forest fires during the 2019-2021 period were limited.

citations.text: The audit team visited an agricultural supplies retailer holding wood and WPM and a supermarket holding WPM, both located in the buffer zone, and witnessed the controls carried out by ASAE. Inspectors stated that apart from carrying out controls in line with the ASAE centrally designed plan they also carry out unannounced inspections controlling the compliance of different operators with very wide range of legislation and that they write a report when they detect non-compliances or infringements. They also stated that they had attended targeted training and were carrying out controls on wood and WPM based on a manual with standard operating procedures and specific information concerning the WPM and the situation in the buffer zone. During the inspections the audit team noted that: · The business operators met were not aware of the national and EU legal requirements relevant to WPM used for the packaging of commodities they receive. They were advised during the visit of the audit team about the measures that they should take if consignments packed on non-compliant pallets or other WPM were to arrive; · In one case, inspectors did not cross-check the registration numbers of marked WPM against any list of heat treatment companies provided by the DGAV as required by the inspection procedures implemented by ASAE In addition, they had 19 not raised any concerns about the presence of pallets, which were not ISPM 15 marked and had been stored on the premises for many years. As a result they could not verify that the requirements of Article 10 of Decision 2012/535/EU were complied with; · In a second case, inspectors, despite having the documented procedures in hand, were unable to identify non-compliance due to inaccurate and/or illegible ISPM 15 marks. Following the observations and comments made by the audit team, the non- compliant pallets and WPM were seized and were not to be moved until they were sent for treatment, safe disposal or destruction.

Controls of movements of susceptible material are carried out at different stages in the supply and transport chain. Appropriate action is taken in the event of a non-compliance or an interception. However, the controls of retailers in the buffer zone are not adequate to identify the movement of potentially non-compliant WPM. 5.6 Authorisation and supervision of heat treatment facilities and marking in accordance with ISPM 15 Legal requirements Articles 13, 14, 15 and 16 of Decision 2012/535/EU Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that the CA has the information necessary regarding all orchards in a DA, in order to be able to control that these are subject to phytosanitary measures necessary to eradicate a Union quarantine pest from the areas concerned, as required under Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. and

citations.text: The DGAV informed the audit team that according to the national Decree Law, professional operators carrying out the activities referred to in Article 65(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, in Portugal, are obliged to be registered in a register kept by, or accessible by, the DGAV, and shared a summary list of registered operators to the audit team. Other operators, such as producers of citrus fruits (orchards) are registered under agricultural legislation, but the DGAV does not have direct access to those registers.

According to Article 65 referred to above, Member States may decide for further categories of operators to be registered if so justified by the pest risk presented by the plants that they grow. Portugal has not yet made use of that possibility, but the DGAV informed the audit team that this is currently being considered. 5.5.2 Measures in case of suspicion of Trioza erytreae

The DGAV informed the audit team that the DRAPs shall locate and map abandoned host trees and orchards in the BZ and in the surveillance zone. The DRAPs however do not have access to information about active orchards in the DAs. This was confirmed during an on-site visit in a DA, when the DRAP showed the audit team a citrus orchard which they knew of only because its owner reported a suspected case of infestation with T. erytreae to the DRAP. The suspicion was later confirmed, and measures such as phytosanitary treatments, pruning and placing of yellow traps were applied in the orchard. The orchard was in an existing DA when the owner reported the suspected finding.

The CA does not have access to information about active orchards in DAs or elsewhere, and therefore cannot check that phytosanitary measures are carried out in orchards, as required. This potentially undermines the measures for eradication taken in a DA.

citations.text: The DGAV informed the audit team that national legislation provides the possibility to impose penalties on private individuals for not implementing the required eradication measures. However, the DRAPs do not have measures in place to enable them to immediately take the necessary phytosanitary measures in cases when these are not carried out by the owner or any other person on behalf of the owner. In such cases, the matter must first be taken to court, although the DGAV stated that they had never taken private individuals to court for failing to implement the eradication measures. One DRAP further stated that this would be time consuming and that they would not have the resources needed. This means that measures to eradicate Union quarantine pests may not be taken immediately, as required by Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. 13

The CA cannot immediately take measures to eradicate T. erytreae in private gardens unless the owners cooperate voluntarily. Given the large number of host plants present in private gardens, this situation potentially risks undermining efforts made by the CA and professional operators to eradicate the pest and increases the risk for its further spread.

recommendations.text: Ensure that competent authorities have access to a sufficient number of suitably qualified staff and adequate laboratory capacity for timely implementation of official controls and other official activities for Xylella fastidiosa as required by Article 5(1) (d) and (e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. to 37, 51 and 52.

citations.text: The audit team noted that: · The designation of Fitolab was in line with provisions of Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 following a series of audits by DGAV and the NRL. The NRL supervises the activity of the designated laboratory in line with EU rules; · In 2020 and 2021 there were significant delays in the completion of the Xf tests by the NRL due to the lack of human resources and the limited availability of PCR reagents. In 2021, the NRL analysed 8,096 plant and insect samples for Xf, 79 of them tested positive. At the time of the audit the laboratory had a weekly capacity for 250 samples with a theoretical response time of 7-15 days, which were significantly longer in the main sampling periods in 2021; · The designation of Fitolab provided additional capacities, however the response time for samples from the DA averages 28 days due to the available laboratory capacities and other technical aspects; · The delays in the completion of the laboratory tests contributed to the delays in the implementation of the eradication measures (see section 5.5.1). Due to the reasons above it is considered by the audit team that the laboratory capacity issues present at the time of the 2020 audit have not been fully addressed. Conclusions on the organisational aspects of Xf controls

The applied methodology and the laboratories' participation in proficiency tests provide assurances regarding the reliability of test results. Although the designated laboratories have initiated procedures for accreditation to EN ISO/IEC 17025, this process was not finalised and therefore the required guarantees for the analytical performance are not 7 provided. Delays in completing the laboratory tests can compromise the timely implementation of the eradication measures.

In relation to the inventory of the plants to be removed in the IZs, the audit team noted during the site visits that: · The work is carried out by DRAP or ICNF inspectors. This activity is particularly difficult and time consuming in the Porto DA, due to the very high number of plant species/genera tested positive for Xf subspecies multiplex; · CA inspectors possessed the necessary botanical knowledge. For the identification of unknown species, a publicly accessible internet application was used. The number and geographical location of the identified plants is duly recorded on the IT platform; · Access issues in steep or inaccessible parts of the IZs and legal access rights to some private properties significantly hindered or made it impossible to complete the inventories.

In the infected zones of the Porto outbreaks there are very long delays in the identification and removal of plants, specified by the EU legislation, due to lack of inspection, administrative and plant removal capacities, difficulties in identifying and notifying the landowner and in accessing sites. Consequently, the eradication of Xf is very unlikely and there is a considerable risk of spread of the disease within the DAs and to other parts of the country.

The 2021 statistically based surveys in the BZs were planned fully in line with the provisions of the EU legislation. Due to staff shortages, many of the selected sites were not checked in the Porto and Lisbon BZs. In addition, and in particular in the Porto BZs the territory of the selected sites could not be inspected entirely due to access issues. Therefore, the minimum requirements of the EU legislation for the surveys were not met and the actual extent of the outbreak is not known in those areas. This prevents the proper implementation of the eradication measures. In the Tavira BZ the surveys were completed in line with the EU rules.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the laboratories are not accredited in accordance with the standard EN ISO/IEC 17025, although it is required by Article 37(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. It is expected that the accredited status will be achieved in the first semester of 2022.

citations.text: A DGAV guidance document requires vector collection by net sweeping in 10% of the survey squares allocated to the participating organisations. The preferred collection time is late spring and early autumn. However, no further guidance is provided about how to select the allocated squares to be checked, e.g., to prefer the sites located in the vicinity 17 of the IZs with delayed plant removals. The collected insects are processed as described in Section 5.5.2.

In the Porto BZs, DRAP and ICNF carried out vector collections. No positives were found. None of the vectors collected in the Lisbon and Tavira BZs by DRAP tested positive. Philaenus spumarius, the main vector of Xf in the EU was not collected during the surveys in Tavira. 5.5.4 Measures against vectors

recommendations.text: Legal basis: Articles 13 and 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 Recommendation based on conclusion: 19 Associated finding: 16, 17 and 18 iew the designation of remote areas so that they meet the definition laid down in EU legislation.

citations.text: Domestic legislation authorises, throughout the country, on-site burial of animal carcasses and Category 2 material, consisting of ABP from on-farm slaughter, provided that the amount does not exceed 40 kg a week. This is not in line with EU rules, in particular Article 13 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, which do not provide for any exemption for routinely burying these types of ABP (outside of remote areas).

For bovine animals, an authorisation from DGAV (regional services) is required before on-farm slaughter takes place; animals must be younger than 12 months and the number of slaughters is limited to two per year. As part of the authorisation process, DGAV must verify that ABP from such slaughter is collected by an authorised ABP operator. In one of the regions visited, where more than 800 authorisations were granted between 2019 and 2022, the abovementioned rules were enforced. In the other region visited, where between 10 to 20 authorisations were given on an annual basis, the on-farm slaughter was in certain cases authorised without any prior check that ABP would be collected by an authorised ABP operator.

In one of the regions visited, official controls identified that ABP from the treatment of hides by tanneries (before the tanning process) were incorrectly disposed of as municipal waste, contrary to Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. DGAV informed the audit team that, to date, no solution had been found to process such material in Portugal. Category 3 (and Category 1) processing plants were not willing to accept these by- products from hides due to difficulties in processing them. Consequently, at the time of the audit, such ABP were not disposed of in line with ABP rules. Conclusions on the system in place for collection, use and disposal of ABP and DP

The system in place for collection, treatment and disposal of ABP is largely capable of ensuring a safe management of ABP an DP. However, ABP from the treatment of hides are not disposed of in line with EU rules and some ABP from on-farm slaughter are disposed of by burial, while this is not authorised under EU rules for ABP.

citations.text: Domestic legislation defines the areas that have been categorised as `remote' under Article 19(1)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In mainland Portugal, five geographical areas are designated as `remote'. The reasons being that these areas have low density of animal population, include natural parks or mountains and, because of their geography, present collection difficulties and are distant from establishments for processing and disposal of ABP. In these areas, on-the-spot burial of bovine, ovine, caprine, and porcine animals is authorised. However, within these remote areas, burial of dead animals is not authorised for holdings considered intensive and for dead bovine animals aged 48 months and over.

Based on discussions held with the ABP operator managing collection of fallen stock in the northern and central parts of Portugal, collection is possible in most areas, except those 5 where trucks have no physical access. In addition, the fact that ABP are collected from farms with intensive animal production located in remote areas implies that trucks have access to, at least, part of these areas. Therefore, since there are viable collection and transports arrangements in parts of the areas categorised as `remote', such areas do not meet the definition of a `remote area' in Article 3(23) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

The designation of some areas as `remote' is not fully justified since means of collection operate in parts of these areas. In addition, the total bovine animal population located in such areas exceeds, by far, the maximum authorised under EU rules.

audits.title: Slaughter hygiene and meat inspection requirements

recommendations.text: The central competent authority should ensure that the relevant guidelines concerning the poultry meat sector (including those related to ante-mortem inspection at the holding of provenance) are updated to ensure that they are in line with the requirements of relevant EU legislation.

citations.text: However, the audit team noted that the guidance on ante-mortem inspection (AMI) of poultry at the holding of provenance (DGAV Order 23/G/2016) allows that "approved veterinarians" perform AMI at the holding of origin (EU legislation requires that AMI should be carried out by an official veterinarian (OV)). In this regard, DGAV informed the audit team that this document had been in place before the new EU legislation was applicable and it has not been updated as yet. They explained that the procedure was applied in the past, and in a small number of slaughterhouses due to the lack of available human resources. They added that this option is no longer practiced, as additional OVs have since been employed, and that, in any case, DGAV intends to amend the provisions contained in this document in order to bring them in line with EU requirements.

National legislation and guidelines necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector are in place and they are largely in line with EU legislation, with the exception of one guideline, which was not up-to-date and, as a result, certain provisions of its content are contrary to EU legislation.

According to national rules, AMI of poultry can be done at slaughterhouse by OVs or, when necessary, at the holding of origin by approved veterinarians. DGAV explained that "when necessary" means when the CAs detect a lack of OVs at a specific slaughterhouse for a particular day or period. In this regard, there is a specific procedure under Order 23/G/2016 (see paragraph 3), which describes the steps to follow and, among other things, requires OAs to perform a simplified AMI under the responsibility of the OV. DGAV added that at the time of this audit this procedure was not being applied in any slaughterhouse and AMI is always carried out by OVs at the slaughterhouse.

responses.response: DGAV Despatch 23/G/2016 will be repealed and Chapter III ted to Part A of the Poultry Meat Inspection Manual (on ante-mortem inspection) will be adapted to remove the references to this despatch and to AMI in the holding of provenance. The repeal document is being prepared. The amendments are expected to be completed by the end of June 2022. Page: 1

citations.text: DGAV receives prior notification of all feed imports. In case of GM feed materials, the operators are obliged to complete a GMO declaration, identifying the corresponding events. recommendations.text: The competent authorities should increase the qualification of the inspectors involved in official controls by providing them with the relevant training (i.e. training regarding Listeria monocytogenes testing, cross-contamination, critical control points) in order to ensure effective and appropriate official controls as required by Article 5(4)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted that packed and uncovered lettuce was stored in a cold store for a few hours before dispatch. Condensation dripping from a part of the ceiling was observed. This was not spotted by the inspectors as a potential source of contamination with Listeria monocytogenes.

The audit team found that, generally, non-compliances present were identified and reported; some shortcomings had, however, not been noted: · the audit team noted some shortcomings regarding the defined critical limits in the HACCP plans, which had not been identified by the CA; · inability on the inspectors' part to assess the efficacy of operators' own-check systems regarding microbiological risks, in particular regarding the presence of Listeria monocytogenes during processing. Inspectors were not familiar with the sampling of contact surfaces in line with the EU Reference Laboratory's guidelines regarding the right time, place and sampling tools to be used. Inspectors stated that they did not feel sufficiently trained to assess these own-controls effectively. · potential cross-contamination by workers, e.g. produce dropped on the floor and was put back on the transport belt, and workers did not change gloves after touching the floor. Condensation on ceilings over exposed produce was not always detected and dealt with efficiently. Inspectors did not note that clean and dirty crates were stored beside each other, which could lead to cross-contamination or the mixing up of clean and dirty crates. Sprout-producing establishments

The audit team visited the third operator and accompanied the inspectors during their annual control visit. The inspectors used the checklist in place and detected multiple non- compliances · visible gaps around some of the doors between the processing rooms and the exterior, which could allow rodents and insects to enter; · several flycatchers were full of insects and not serviced in time; · dirty and rusty tools, dirty walls, sinks in bad condition, condensation on ceilings; · use of sprouting containers not fit for food contact; · use of duct tape to repair tools in contact with the final product; · dirty containers washed in a high-risk area; · contact surface samples for Listeria monocytogenes were taken once a year but only after cleaning. 13

During official controls of FNAO the inspectors in all regions visited used the harmonised national checklists. This allows a uniform way of monitoring official controls in this sector. However, without sufficiently comprehensive background knowledge regarding Listeria monocytogenes, inspectors could overlook aspects relevant to the prevention of this particular microbiological risks.

Regarding processing plants, inspections were carried out according to plan. Nonetheless, not all aspects were controlled effectively, impacting in turn on the effectiveness of the official controls in ensuring correction of all deficiencies identified. 5.2.5 Official sampling procedures Legal requirements Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. audits.title: Official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that the designated border control posts comply with the minimum requirements for border control posts appropriate to the categories of animals and goods for which the post has been designated.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3 to 8 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the facilities in place for official controls on live animals and goods of animal origin at the BCP Lisbon airport were generally compliant with the requirements for BCP's, in line with Article 64(3) of the OCR and Articles 3, 4, 5 and 6 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. However, the team found that the facilities in place for official controls on goods of non-animal origin were not compliant with those minimum requirements, and noted the following shortcomings: · there were no storage facilities for food of non-animal origin, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · adjacent commercial storage facilities of cargo handlers were used for storage of food of non-animal origin, including detained and rejected consignments. The team visited the facilities of one such cargo handler and noted that conditions for the hygienic storage of goods were not in place, and that there was no lockable or fenced off area for goods presenting a risk, which is not in line with Article 3(12) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · there were no storage rooms for consignments of feed of non-animal origin requiring temperature control, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted that facilities in place at the inspection centres Sotogus and Liscont as part of the port BCP Lisbon were not compliant with the requirements laid down in Articles 64(3) of the OCR and Articles 3, 4, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. The following shortcomings were noted during the visits to the two inspection centres: 12 · both inspection centres did not have adequate drainage in the unloading, inspection and storage areas or rooms, which is not in line with Article 3(2) and (3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · at the inspection centre Sotagus, the storage room for ambient goods of animal origin intended for human consumption was not easy to clean and disinfect due to the presence of a wooden floor, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · at the inspection centre Sotagus, there were no storage facilities for food of non- animal origin, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · at the inspection centre Liscont, storage rooms were in place for food of non- animal origin, however their use was not authorised by Customs. Consequently, no storage facilities were available for food of non-animal origin, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · at the inspection centre Liscont, the inspection room for food of non-animal origin which was adjacent to those storage rooms was poorly maintained and was therefore not easy to clean and disinfect, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the inspection room did not have a supply of hot water and was not equipped with the necessary equipment for sampling of goods, which is not in line with Articles 3(1)(b) and 4(2) respectively of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; · as regards the facilities for feed of non-animal origin, there was no storage room for frozen consignments at the inspection centre Sotagus, while there were no storage rooms for chilled or frozen consignments at the inspection centre Liscont, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team noted in the case of the BCP Setubal port, based on their evaluation of the assessment table and supporting documents provided, that that there were no storage facilities for food of non-animal origin, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

While the evaluated BCPs were generally compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs for the categories of animals and goods of animal origin for which they had been designated, shortcomings were identified with respect to the facilities in place at three BCPs, for the storage of goods of non-animal origin intended for human consumption for which the BCPs had been designated, which have the potential to reduce the overall effectiveness of the official control system.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that non-compliances are followed up in a timely and effectively way in line with point 1(a) of Article 5 of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the DGAV control system rewards operators that demonstrate better compliance with food safety rules. The audit team noted in particular that: a. the control system does not require the follow up of non-compliances in the categories GC1 and GC2 before the next scheduled control. The operators are not obliged to communicate corrective measures to the CA; b. inspection reports showed that numerous non-compliances in the category GC2 were detected at some operators. Several of these had not been rectified by the time of the next scheduled control. This did not trigger an infringement procedure nor the application of a GC3 non-compliance, as foreseen in the CA instructions. Furthermore, a high number of GC2 non-compliances does not change the compliance category of the operator; c. in one region, 80% of the controls were conducted with prior announcement (one day or more in advance). The SIPACE statistics for that region showed that the detection rate for GC3 and GC4 non-compliances were considerably higher if the controls were unannounced. The CA stated, that this is related to staff shortage and to avoid no-shows at operators.

The inspection reports of one operator highlighted the fact that some activities carried out were not within the scope of approval, and this situation was not remedied by the time of the next scheduled inspection. No other measures were taken, and it took several years from the initial report of the non-compliance before the approval was amended to cover these activities.

Furthermore, the official controls had gaps, as the inspectors had not identified: a. weaknesses in the design and the implementation of operators' good hygiene practices and HACCP; b. nonadherence to temperature requirements for fresh and frozen fishery products; c. the lack of awareness of operators with regard to their obligations relating to food that is not in compliance with food safety requirements and the circumstances 10 under which they need to inform the CAs thereof.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all operators in the fishery product production chain inform the competent authorities about food which is not in compliance with food safety requirements in line with Article 19(3) of Regulation EC 178/2002. a.

citations.text: The establishments visited during the audit were, in general, of a satisfactory standard regarding structure, hygiene conditions and equipment. Nevertheless, some shortcomings were noted, which were not spotted by official controls: a. Operators are not always aware of the circumstances under which they need to notify DGAV and/or ASAE about food that is not in compliance with food safety requirements. This is an obligation laid down in Article 19(1) of the General Food Law (5). In one case, imported frozen sardines were sampled by the operator and the analytical results showed an exceedance of histamine. The consignment of 8 700 kg was destroyed by landfill in cooperation with the local municipality. Neither the operator nor the municipality informed DGAV or ASAE about it. Therefore, no follow-up measures could be carried out by the CA (e.g. issuing a RASFF notification); b. At two establishments visited, fishery products were treated with a mixture of E- 330, E-331 and hydrogen peroxide to change their colour. However, both the operator and CA regarded this use as an additive acceptable, on the basis that the technical fiche describes hydrogen peroxide as a suitable processing aid. (5) Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 January 2002 laying down the general principles and requirements of food law, establishing the European Food Safety Authority and laying down procedures in matters of food safety. 9 c. A factory vessel was visited 2 days after landing. The fish holds were sealed by DRM and not available for inspection. The work floor visited had hygiene shortcomings (dirty conveyor belts and machines, leaking hydraulic tubes above the production line (despite an attempted `quick-fix'), general poor hygiene). DGAV staff stated that the vessel would be inspected before departure; d. At one establishment: the thawing of frozen sardines before processing was not controlled regarding the time/temperature process. The temperatures of some sardines were measured as above 4.1°C. The operator was to maintain the fish at ambient temperature for another 12 hours. The process was not described (and therefore, not validated) in the HACCP plan. This could potentially lead to elevated histamine levels; e. At a cold store: temperatures above -15°C were recorded for a number of weeks; f. One establishment used borehole water which was treated with chlorate. The water was checked twice a day internally. The operators stated that the intended concentration would be 0.2 to 0.6 ppm. Sample values showed a concentration of 0.1 ppm in several cases. There was no written standard operating procedure in place to describe the acceptable limits and associated corrective actions when these limits were exceeded; g. Municipality water is monitored by the water supply companies, and test results were available. If the source of the water is from the operators own well, the water used in the establishment must be treated and controlled by the operator in accordance with the provisions of Decree-Law 69/2023. DGAV stated, that the verification of compliance regarding water standards is not their responsibility; h. The audit team did not find evidence that water and/or ice used by operators from their own well/s, is under official controls; i. Unlabelled white boxes were noted in one cold store. The goods were not owned by the operator, who was not aware of their responsibility that all goods present in their establishment must comply with hygiene and other rules, such as labelling; j. Exposed wood was in contact with fishery products. Conclusions on official controls on the production and placing on the market

Furthermore, the official controls had gaps, as the inspectors had not identified: a. weaknesses in the design and the implementation of operators' good hygiene practices and HACCP; b. nonadherence to temperature requirements for fresh and frozen fishery products; c. the lack of awareness of operators with regard to their obligations relating to food that is not in compliance with food safety requirements and the circumstances 10 under which they need to inform the CAs thereof.

audits.title: evaluate controls on residues of pharmacologically active substances, pesticides and contaminants in animals and animal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that the residue control plans are implemented fully in line with pertinent EU requirements and planned arrangements. Relevant EU legislation: Annex III to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1644, Annexes I and II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1646, and Annex I to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/932.

citations.text: In recent years, the implementation of residue control started only in the second half of the year, which is not in line with EU requirements (20) and did not allow the fulfilment of the plans and of the minimum sampling frequencies laid down in EU legislation (21), even if the competent authority always planned 0.5% more samples than required by EU legislation.
In 2023, only 4077 (62%) of the 6574 planned samples were taken, out of which 3588 samples were analysed by the laboratories, therefore only 55% of the samples planned were taken and analysed.

In 2024, the sampling plans were transmitted to the regional offices in September, and 4911 (74%) of the 6654 planned samples were taken, and 4631 samples were analysed, therefore only 70% of the samples planned were taken and analysed. In addition, 70% of all samples were taken in October and November, which is not in line with EU legislation (22) to ensure an even spread of sampling throughout the year.

A total of 280 taken samples in 2024 could not be analysed in the laboratory analysing most samples. For four of the 280 samples, transport-related matters were indicated as the reason, for 70 ­ sampling-related obstacles and for 206 ­ the laboratory highlighted breakdowns of the technical equipment and staff holidays and shortages. In June 2025, the competent authority cancelled the request of analysis for 44 samples taken in 2024, as the analyses had still not started.

For both years 2023 and 2024, the auditors observed that, in addition to the sampling carried out largely in the second half of those years, in several cases, multiple sampling was performed to fulfil the requested sample numbers, especially during the last weeks of the respective years. This multiple sampling was not always performed in line with EU legal requirements which set the conditions to be respected for double sampling. Notably, no specific identification of the operator could be found, nor any risk-based justification. This appeared to be done only to improve overall sample numbers at the end of the year. There was no other justification (23).
Other deficiencies in the implementation of the plan, such as incorrect matrices sampled, could not be corrected on time, as they were only discovered when the sampling year was already over.

In addition, the turn-around times between the arrival of the sample and the availability of the analytical result from the laboratory in charge of most analyses, exceeded, for most of the samples, the 30 days agreed with the competent authority. In the 2023 and 2024 sample files verified by the auditors, several delays of 6-8 months were observed before the analytical result was available. At the time of the audit, there was no systematic verification by the competent authority regarding the turn-around times of samples in the laboratory.

For 2025, the sampling plans were distributed to the regional offices by email on 5 May 2025. Until the time of the audit, 2552 (39%) of the 6506 samples planned were taken by 6 October 2025, out of which 746 were registered as analysed. In the same laboratory, as mentioned in the previous finding, the auditors were informed that for 324 of the 1572 analysed samples (all plans), the turn-around time already exceeded 30 days. The laboratory explained the reasons for these delays as linked to staff holidays, staff shortages and breakdowns of technical equipment. (22) Point 1 of Annex III to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1644. (23) Point 8 of Annex III to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1644. 5

The responsibilities of the competent authorities involved, and the regional sample distribution procedures are the same as indicated for the national risk-based control plan (see findings 2, 3 and 4).

In 2023, while all planned samples were taken, 92% were analysed. While there is a clear designation of competent authorities and distribution of the tasks, and the sampling officials are adequately trained and equipped, the overall effectiveness of the residue control plans for pharmacologically active substances and contaminants is seriously undermined by incomplete implementation of the plans combined with uneven distribution of the sampling over the year.

audits.title: assess the controls on Antimicrobial veterinary medicinal products

recommendations.text: To ensure that the controls required by Article 123 of Regulation (EU) 2019/6 also verify that antimicrobials or groups of antimicrobials listed in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1255 are not used in animals. The competent authority's response to the recommendation can be found at: http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/rep_details_en.cfm?rep_inspection_ref=CT-2025-0054

citations.text: There are no specific controls to check that antimicrobials in the reserved list referred to in Article 37(5) are not used. DGAV does not conduct controls on veterinarians practicing with companion animals to check this point and PEMV allows the issuing of prescriptions containing these medicines. In addition, (human) pharmacies retailing VMPs are inspected by the human medicines inspectorate, which does not include checks on the dispensing of these substances during their inspections. This is not in line with Article 123(1) and (2). DGAV stated that they will take steps this year to ensure that PEMV does not issue prescriptions containing substances in the reserved list above.

Except in the case of checks to verify compliance with Article 37(5) concerning the `reserved' antimicrobials listed in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1255, controls on the prescription and use of antimicrobials are well designed and implemented.
